items.title: Is the Populist Moment Over?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Throughout history, a familiar pattern has shown itself: Political elites lose touch with the people over whom they rule, and those people rebel in one way or another. But eventually a new kind of elite asserts itself. The rise of Donald Trump as a political force more than a decade ago was part of one such global wave of anti-elite sentiment. If the midterm results signal the end of the Trump era, do they also signal the beginning of the end of our populist moment? In this episode of The Permanent Questions , Fareed Zakaria joins David Brooks to discuss the history of liberal democracy and the inevitable reactions against it, why technology makes this reaction different from others, and the ways in which our liberal elite will have to change if they want to own the future. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: Today on The Permanent Questions we’re going to talk about a permanent problem. It is that great nations fall when elites get too distanced from the masses and lose popular legitimacy. Here are some examples: The Roman empire in the fifth century, the French monarchy in the 18th century, the Russian aristocracy in the early 20th century, and the shah’s Iran in 1979. There is increasing economic inequality. There’s increasing social inequality. The elites have grown insular and condescending toward the people. They become self-indulgent and corrupt. The elites break the social contract with the people, and the people withdraw their trust and any sense of legitimacy. It seems to me that the United States and many other societies around the globe have been flirting with this kind of catastrophe for many decades. Millions of people have lost faith in the elites, in institutions, in the future, and in each other. These losses of faith produce populist backlashes, and that’s what we’ve been living through over the past 15 years or so. Populist leaders have arisen in societies across the world. Nations on nearly every continent have their own version of Donald Trump. But it turns out that the populists can be guilty of all the sins people associate with the old elite. In fact, they can be more corrupt, more incompetent, more morally bankrupt, more out of touch than the people they promised to replace. When that happens, the voters want to throw the populace out too, and I believe that’s what happened in the American election of 2026. So the million-dollar questions become: What comes next? Can leaders in either party reform themselves and win back the trust of the people? Can we restore the kind of popular legitimacy that any nation needs to function okay? Most immediately, are we past peak populism? Have the winds shifted so much that a new historical era is possible? And if so, what’s it going to look like? I’ve asked Fareed Zakaria to join as we wrestle with these questions. Fareed is the host of Fareed Zakaria GPS , CNN’s global-affairs show. He writes a weekly column in The Washington Post . He’s the author of many celebrated and influential books, including The Future of Freedom , The Post-American World , In Defense of a Liberal Education , and most recently, Age of Revolutions: Progress and Backlash From 1600 to the Present . He’s one of the most profound thinkers in the world today, and so I’m pleased to welcome Fareed Zakaria to this table. Fareed Zakaria: Such a pleasure, David. Brooks: Yes, I’m sure it’s the honor of your life. Zakaria: Honestly, to have a conversation with you is a pleasure and an honor. Brooks: You can call me anytime. So one of the things I loved about your most recent book, The Age of Revolutions , is that you describe how liberal societies were built in the first place. Some of your examples are the Netherlands and their golden age, the British golden age, America, and some of the others. I thought that might be useful as we think about where we are as liberal societies, and especially where we are in this moment of, I think, rebuilding. Hopefully, an upcoming moment of rebuilding. My point of view, as you know, is that this election was so big that we could say, maybe not globally, but in the U.S. at least, not only is Trumpism over, but we’ve passed peak populism. That’s a bit of an optimistic assumption. Now, you have a more global perspective than I do. Do you agree with that? Zakaria: So I think in every way—if you look in the book, every one of these liberal experiments, you tend to see a backlash. At some point people say, “This is too much change. We’re moving too far away from the traditions, the mooring, the community, the old faith of our fathers.” And you get a backlash. Then the question becomes how society handles that backlash. Does it find a way to rebuild, as you say, or does it end up getting mired in a certain kind of dysfunction? The French Revolution being the best example of it not working out. I think where we are is still in that backlash to 30 or 40 years of globalization, massive economic and technological change, enormous cultural change—the rise of women, the rise of minorities, immigration being the kind of symbolic aspect of that change. But I do think you’re right that in America we have now seen something interesting, which is Trump 2.0 was a much more pure implementation of right-wing populism than Trump 1.0. People forget that in the first Trump term, there was a lot of Paul Ryan and Steve Mnuchin and a lot of the old kind of Republican Party still at work. Trump 2 was all populism, and it (a) didn’t work—manufacturing employment is not back in America—and (b) the public didn’t like it. So there is a kind of sense that: Okay, these guys might have been pointing to a problem that was real, but they don’t have the solution . Now, where that goes, I’m not as certain as you—and I know you’re saying it with optimism—because the ball is in the Democrats’ court. Can they craft a new vision that isn’t just taking advantage of this rejection? If they can’t, I do think there’s still enough life in the idea that we have to reject these open borders, open trade; we gotta look out for the working class. Populism at some level, particularly right-wing populism, is a kind of politics of nostalgia. It’s saying, “I know the world has been changing so much. I’m going to take you back. I’m going to take you back to when it was all more comfortable.” And that’s still a very powerful appeal. We still pine for the Garden of Eden. And there are all these politicians, whether it’s in Brexit, whether it’s Marine Le Pen in France, who are promising that. What we have had in America—the big good fortune, if you think of it that way—is that we had a very pure attempt to implement these ideas, and it didn’t work. Brooks: I think that’s a good way to phrase it, because it reminds the Democrats Donald Trump happened for a reason, and they still have to deal with that reason. But to put my more blindly optimistic spin on things: Whenever I ask people, “What made you who you are?,” it’s always some moment of rupture and repair. Something bad happened; they had to tear down parts of their life, and then they had to rebuild. And I think that’s happened in our personal lives, and I think it happens in national lives. And now this—I’m a little abashed to be quoting Samuel Huntington to you. Tell me: Let’s make clear who Samuel Huntington was to you. Explain who he was. Zakaria: So Samuel Huntington was a professor at Harvard, probably the most influential political scientist of the second half of the 20th century. He wrote incredibly important books in almost every field of political science, comparative politics, American politics, international relations. Most famous for his book The Clash of Civilizations . And he was my academic mentor. He was the chairman of my dissertation committee, but we also had a close personal relationship. He was an extraordinary guy. Very proper WASP gentleman, and I was this ethnic Indian immigrant, but somehow we got on amazingly well. Brooks: And now I look back on him with sort of a reverence veering toward awe. Even the books of his I did not like were prescient. So anyway, I bring up Huntington because I think in 1983, when you were probably not yet there, he wrote a book with a very boring title, I think it was called America’s Promise or— Zakaria: American Politics: The Promise of Disharmony . That was it. And I’m guessing you’re going to quote the last line. Brooks: What was the last line? Zakaria: It’s a great last line. He says, “The critics of America say America is a lie. It is not a lie. It is a disappointment, but it can only be a disappointment because it is [also] a hope.” Brooks: The part I cottoned onto—I read it in 2020 during COVID; I’m stuck at home. And at some point in that book, he says, I’ve noticed this weird pattern in American history, that every couple generations —I don’t know if it’s 60 years, whatever—America goes through what he calls “a moral convulsion.” People want to burn everything down. The passionate generation comes on the scene. There’s a new form of communications technology. And those moral convulsions are horrific to live through. And he pointed to the American Revolutionary period 1770s; Andrew Jackson 1830s; the 1890s, when we sort of failed at industrialization and then succeeded. The 1960s—people forget how brutal the ’60s were. There were thousands of bombings. And he says, I don’t know if I believe in this pattern, but if it holds, sometime around the second decade of the 21st century, America will go through another moral convulsion. I’m sitting there in 2020 surrounded by all that, and I’m thinking, Well done, Professor Huntington. And the good news is you come out of them. It’s that process of rupture and repair. And so I believe that we had to learn what Trump, what MAGA had to teach us. But I think Democrats have learned a lot of it—not all of them, and some have learned nothing. But on immigration, I think they’ve learned, on the fact that we were ignoring the working class. And so to me, it would be totally normal that we would go through a historical pivot, because we’ve gone through so many. Jared Diamond wrote a book about international pivots; I think called Upheaval . So sometimes countries just decline, but as long as countries have vitality, they can come right back, and I think we’re at one of those moments. Zakaria: I tend to share your optimism about that, and I’ll tell why it is. Firstly, as an immigrant, I see the vitality, right? I came to this country because of that vitality. It still has it in spades. Just look at the tech sector. But don’t even just look at the tech sector. I’m struck by how Americans—you know, one of the things I always notice about America is we really wash our dirty laundry in public. We talk every problem through. But that very act is in a sense not just cathartic, but you’re searching for solutions. And the solutions are many and myriad, and the problem is large and centralized, so you don’t see the solutions, but they bubble up from the bottom. And that’s one of the geniuses of America—this bottom-up vitality, often in smaller communities, that then moves up. And I think we’re beginning to see that because, as you say, we now know some of the problems, but it’s also because centrally America is a country that is the embodiment of Enlightenment liberalism. And what is Enlightenment liberalism, at the end of the day? It is that human beings should have the autonomy, the choice, the dignity, and the freedom to live the kind of life that gives them the satisfaction, the happiness, the pursuit of happiness that they want, and that’s a very powerful idea. At the end of the day, that’s what people want. Yeah, they would like community, and yeah, they would like—but they want it if they can choose it. They don’t want it if it’s forced on them. And the problem with so much of the illiberal critique of liberalism is ultimately it becomes coercion, because it’s like: Divorces are bad. Okay, agreed. We should have fewer divorces. Okay, agreed. We should put laws in place that make no-fault divorce harder, right? Traditional marriages are good. Great. We should therefore discourage gays from marrying. Wait, why? In other words, it all turns into: Let me tell you how to live your life . And to me, Enlightenment liberalism has at its core had that Kantian idea that a human being is an end unto himself, not a means to your larger ideological project. You can’t treat him as a pawn in your grand ideological adventure. And that idea will win out in the end. And so at the end of the day, we are going to be a multicultural democracy in this country. We can’t pretend that minorities don’t exist. We can’t pretend that women haven’t realized that they deserve to be first-class citizens. And we’re going to have to find a way to make that work. Brooks: My inner conservative is coming out. So I think the one conservative idea which I think is true is that for liberal institutions which revere choice to work, they have to be based on institutions that are not based on choice. And I would say your family is sort of not—you didn’t choose what family you were born into. For many people, their faith is not really a matter of choice. Their attachment to their town; it doesn’t feel like a choice. If you’re a Bostonian, you are Boston down to your bones. And I would include your moral order. There has to be a shared moral order that you didn’t choose, that it’s just you share with people around you. There’s a historian, George Marsden, who says what gave Martin Luther King’s rhetoric such force was his conviction that right and wrong were woven into the fabric of the universe, that segregation was not just wrong in some times and some places; it was eternally wrong. Slavery is eternally wrong. And I would say the conservative critique of liberalism was, in many cases, they tried to turn covenantal relationships into voluntary transactional relationships, and the most damaging one was the moral order one, where I would say people got too carried away with liberalism—and I’m a liberal, of course—and therefore they weakened that shared sense of moral order. Without that, I can’t trust you, because we don’t agree on what we ought to do. Without that, I don’t even have my own moral philosophy, because most people can’t come up with their own moral philosophy. So what do you think of that conservative critique of liberalism, and that to be liberals we have to preserve those institutions, mostly faith, family, and flag? Zakaria: I 100 percent agree with the conservative critique that you lose something when you do that. I mean, this really began with Nietzsche. Nietzsche pointed out that at the end of the day, if you say God is dead, you have kind of upended the entire universe on which society rested. Walter Lippmann has this great book in the ’20s he writes called A Preface to Morals , where he says, The central dilemma of modern society is we have lost the certainty that came from faith, family, and community, and we have replaced it with nothing . And I think it remains the central dilemma. But here’s the problem: In order to say that you have these things that are not voluntary, not chosen, how do you return to them? Are you going to say that you’re going to force people to attend church? Are you going to say that, again, you’re going to force families to stay together when there are unhappy marriages, when women want to get out? Are you going to make it more difficult for a woman to be able to separate from a husband and live decently? Those were the mechanisms we used. They were all coercive. They were all ones where you denied the individuality and the dignity of people. At the end of the day, people want the autonomy and dignity and freedom as individuals. You can try to persuade them that they should try to think about community and family and faith more. You can tell them: Here’s a way to think about what religion got you, and is there a way to substitute for it with some of the— And frankly, David, you do a lot of that work in the many of the projects you do, but it’s all persuasion. It’s not coercion, and that I think is great. I think a liberal society should be a place where those things happen. Look, I grew up in a much more conservative society. The divorce rate in India today is under 2 percent. Now, do not draw from that the conclusion that everybody in India is happily married. Draw from that the conclusion there are a lot of miserable women in India who are not able to break free of very bad marriages. And so when I hear sometimes these paeans to community and things like that, there’s a part of me that feels like: Can I get an oxygen mask somewhere here? Because I know that those communities often came out of repression, hierarchy, conformism. Brooks: So I offered Huntington; you matched my Huntington and gave me a Lippmann. So I’m going to quote Lippmann back to you. Then I want to get back to my optimism. So Lippmann writes another book called The Public Philosophy , which I think must have been the ’50s and ’60s. And he’s talking about the loss of the moral order that George Marsden had been talking about, and he says, “If what is right and wrong is based on what each individual feels, we are outside the bounds of civilization.” And so my view is of course you can’t force anybody to believe something. You can’t force anybody to get married. But a society can have scripts, and when I went to high school, it was just in my script, in my family, and frankly in my social class: You go to college. And then it was a script: You get married. Or even in high school, there was a script for if you wanted to date somebody—there was a script. And I think a lot of those scripts are gone right now, and I’m not going to force anybody, but I would love to see more scripts. Zakaria: Part of what makes that harder, I think, is that we have entered into a world in which because of technology, there is the possibility of kind of radical individualism. So the world you and I grew up in, there was a common culture, and that common culture produced, I think, in its own way, almost subconsciously a common script, a common moral order, and things like that. And it wasn’t so much religious. I think of it even in terms of the movies we watched, you know? When we were growing up and we were in college—I don’t know, everybody saw the Indiana Jones movies. Everybody saw When Harry Met Sally . Everybody read The Bonfire of the Vanities . There is no such common culture anymore, because everything is sliced and diced. If you have three kids and they vary in age by three or four years each, they will each have found their own little silo of culture, and it’s very hard to talk about common values when everybody is choosing their own thing, and then that is reinforced over and over again. Technology enabled a kind of radical fragmentation of culture and values and morality. And I think that sometimes we underplay the degree to which technology has fractured us as a society. We look at lots of other things, but if it’s technology, how do you un-invent social media and the internet and the thousand channels people can watch? Brooks: You may be right that’s never coming back, but that presents a bigger challenge for those of us who are trying to rebuild a liberal era, which is the challenge of: How do you rebuild liberalism in these circumstances to make it humane? And that strikes me as a very big and very daunting challenge. But to go back to my optimism, I think it’s upon us right now—and one of the things that’s weird about history: There are certain movements; there are tides. Weirdly, you wouldn’t think there’d be global tides of history. We’re a big, diverse world. But there are certain moments where a lot of similar things happened in a lot of different countries all at once. And so I would say in the early 20th century, we had a totalitarian tide. We had the Russian Revolution, Chinese Revolution, Mussolini, Hitler. It just suddenly seemed totalitarianism was a thing, and people forget it was admired. Mussolini was admired. There’s that song, I won’t punish you with my version of it, but— Zakaria: The Cole Porter song ... Brooks: “You’re the Top.” Mussolini was in that song. And then in the ’60s, there’s a liberation movement. We need to throw off oppressive systems, and so you get decolonization in Africa. You get the civil-rights movement. You get feminism. You got social liberalization of the Woodstock. And then in the 1980s and 1990s, you get the neoliberal tide. Not only Thatcher and Reagan, but in his own way, Gorbachev or Deng Xiaoping. They were all neoliberals. And then you had the global populist tide starting in 2010. And so it’s interesting to think in tides. I feel a little guilty saying the populist tide is over, ’cause if I was sitting in France, in Germany, I may not feel that way. But their populists will screw up in their own time. And so then the question is: What’s the next tide? And I do think some sort of 21st-century liberalism is the best thing we offer, and there’s a suspicion about elites, but to me, you shouldn’t totally look at people’s credentials. You should look at how committed they are to liberalism, and those are the people who will somehow try to figure a way out. Zakaria: I largely agree with what you said, and I think the way I would put the populist revolution: If you really want to look at it globally, it is a kind of anti-elite revolution. If you look at places like Turkey with the rise of Erdoğan—you look at India, the rise of Modi—what is striking is these are very different from Western societies. India’s very poor. Turkey’s middle income. It’s Muslim. And yet the common thread is Modi campaigned essentially proudly proclaiming that he was the first man who was going to be prime minister of India who really did not come from an elite background at all, and in fact was very much a man of the people. Now, there were others: Manmohan Singh, the prime minister before him, who actually had been born poorer than Modi. But Modi was right because Manmohan Singh then got a Ph.D., and so he, through kind of social mobility, had moved himself up into the kind of intellectual elite, whereas Modi always said he was a tea seller or his father was a tea seller. I’m not entirely sure that’s true, but he came from very modest background and never got that kind of escalator that elite education gives you. Erdoğan similarly very much came out of a kind of common person. And almost everywhere you see that there is some kind of a reaction against the rise of this meritocratic, technocratic elite that is increasingly—I mean, you’ve written so well about all of this. These are the bourgeois bohemians. These are the people who became the credentialed elites. In many ways, the first time I began to think of it this way, and the perpetuation of them as a kind of class, was an article you wrote, or maybe it’s in that book, about how the matrimonial columns of The New York Times , the wedding announcements, were almost a kind of symbol of the mergers of the upper middle class. Brooks: People literally called it the mergers and acquisitions page. It was Goldman marries, whatever, Skadden Arps. It was Harvard marries Princeton. Phi Beta Kappa marries Phi Beta Kappa, whatever. Zakaria: Exactly, exactly. You began to realize this is a sociological phenomena. What we should have realized was there’s a whole lot of people who don’t go to Harvard and Yale, and don’t work at Goldman Sachs and Deutsche Bank, and they’re going to look at this world and say, “You guys think this is meritocratic, but we’re somehow shut out of it completely. You guys might think that it’s all happening because you’re so smart, but we exist too.” That’s why Trump said something—and sometimes because he is a political genius, he would say these things unintentionally profound—and he said, “I love the poorly educated.” And what in a sense he was giving voice to was that roar of protest against a world not only that is being ordered that way, but where people who are successful believe that not only do they deserve their success, but you know what? If you’re in the bottom half, maybe you deserve your lot as well because after all, I just took the test. I wasn’t born rich. Yeah but we lost that maybe Christian universalism of saying, “We’re all God’s children.” And you got a stroke of good luck and, as you said, at 16 were able to do well on your SATs, and the other person didn’t. And there isn’t a moral distinction between those two people. So I think that piece feels to me like the most powerful critique that populism has provided to our modern liberal societies, and I don’t know what the solution is, because honestly, you do need talented people to run countries and to run societies and to run corporations and to run universities. Is there fundamentally a different system that doesn’t sort the new elite using brains, education, aptitude, talent? Brooks: I think about my years in the elite. I was working for William F. Buckley when I was 21, when we first met. I’m part of the establishment. You can’t be a New York Times columnist for 20 years and not be part of the establishment. And so, I want to get to that question of: How do we raise a better leadership class? But when I look back at my own culpability, I think a couple things I got wrong. First, you had mentioned that mergers and acquisition page, which then became, I think, the first chapter of a book called Bobos in Paradise, which is about the new upper class. And it was about the rise of the educated class. And I wrote a sentence in that book where I said, Unlike previous establishments, this will not become an insular establishment because anybody can get an education and join . That turned out to be one of the most naive sentences I’ve ever written in my life, because they absolutely turned themselves into an insular establishment you could not crack unless you could afford the SAT prep and all the resources that were poured to the children of the educated class. That was the one problem. Second, I don’t think I appreciated at the time how insular we were becoming. And then third, and this is the obvious one, is that in 2015, I wrote 500 columns saying, “Don’t worry, Donald Trump will never get the Republican nomination for president.” I was living in D.C., my social life was here in New York, I was traveling to New Haven. How could I be out of touch with America on the quiet car of the Acela? I don’t think I was totally blind to what was happening. I mean, a lot of my writing has been attacking my fellow establishmentarians, but I think those were the mistakes that I made. Do you think that way? Like, what did I get wrong? What did I not see coming? Zakaria: Oh, sure. I think probably very similar to yours. I thought he could get the nomination, but I thought he would lose the election because I grew up in India and saw the rise of Hindu fundamentalism, so I had seen this kind of anger and this kind of nationalism and a kind of nationalism that is directed toward the other. But I agree. I think that being part of this very insular elite, what I lost sight of was how many people in America felt so disconnected from that world, from that elite. I would look at the average statistics, and I would say, “America’s doing so much better than Europe.” And if you look at the data, it’s really extraordinary that this period that produces populism in America—this kind of right-wing enraged populism, anguish and enraged populism—was a period where the United States outperformed every other advanced economy in the world. The eurozone economy, roughly speaking, and the U.S. economy were the same in 2005. Today, the U.S. economy’s almost twice the size of the eurozone economy. So we’ve done extraordinarily well, but what I didn’t realize was there had been an enormous inequality, that the average concealed an Appalachia which had really collapsed. And I also did not recognize how much of this is not purely about economics. It’s about dignity. It’s about a cultural world that has gone away. I went to one of these towns in Pennsylvania once and was talking to people around and trying to understand what was causing this right-wing populism. The answers I got were fascinating, which was essentially it’s not that people lost their jobs; they lost their lives. Meaning, many of them had found other work, and again, the data shows that unemployment is at a 50-year low right now, roughly speaking. But what happened was in the old days, they had—there was a steel plant. They worked there. But they all worked there, and then they all went to church together, and they all went to the bowling alley together, and they all went to the hardware store. They went to the Kiwanis club together. Now, much of that is not just about, like, the factory went to South Korea. It’s also that they used to go to the movie theater together, but Netflix took the place of the movies. They’d go to the bowling alley, but online gaming took that. So it was a combination of technology and globalization, but the result was they had lost their lives. They had lost the community and then that feeling of dignity that came from having a good job and being a member. And I think I just looked at the numbers and was like, Well, per capita GDP keeps going up , and things like that. And I think a lot of this right-wing populism is at core cultural—a kind of cultural reaction to saying, “My world has collapsed.” The left tends to offer the 10-point Brookings Institution program that says, “Well, we can do a tax credit, and we can give you retraining, and we can ...” And the right says, “I’m going to take you back to before all this happened.” You know, if you think about “Make America Great Again.” The Brexit slogan was “Take back control.” There is a kind of hearkening to an earlier, more simple time. And it’s very powerfully appealing. I mean, there’s a reason we all have that sense of nostalgia. I remember Nikki Haley once tweeted when she was trying her best to do an impersonation of a MAGA politician, she said, “Wasn’t life so much simpler when we were kids?” And I think I did the math, and I thought that would’ve been around 1975 for her, and I’m thinking, Okay, the United States had just lost its first war in history, Vietnam. The president had just been impeached for high crimes and misdemeanors. The oil prices quadrupled . And the economy was so bad you had to invent a term— stagflation —to describe high unemployment and high inflation. Brooks: Crime tripled. Zakaria: But it’s something fascinating. It’s almost evolutionary that you want to go back. You want to think about a time when it was all better. Brooks: We’ve admitted some of our sins. Let’s talk about the question you asked, which was: how to build a better leadership class. And my view, which I hope is yours, maybe, is every society has a leadership class. The idea that you’re going to get away without an elite—that’s not going to happen. Somebody’s gotta run the government, and somebody’s gotta run the big institutions and educational institutions. So I would never want to go back to the establishment of 1950, because you and I would not be sitting at tables like this one. Zakaria: Exactly. Brooks: But I think they had a couple of advantages that we could learn from but not replicate. The first is they read Plutarch. Like, how do you create a leadership class that’s going to govern well? This has been a problem thought about for thousands of years. Well, read Plutarch. Read the greats. Read Thucydides. Read Clausewitz. Read Sun Tzu. There are great wisdom literature in how to be a leader and what your responsibilities are. This podcast is an attempt to bring back some of that kind of humanistic learning. The second thing is to tell people, “You’re the elite. You have responsibilities.” Zakaria: Act like it. Brooks: Act like it. If FDR was sitting there in—where’d he go? Groton or Choate, one of those schools. Zakaria: Groton. Brooks: And his headmaster was telling him that. Zakaria: Endicott Peabody. Brooks: Exactly. But today, you go to—I don’t want to single out one school—to an elite institution. It’s like, You’re oppressed; you’re marginalized. You poor Harvard students . So they’re not told that. But then the third thing that they had the advantage of was, at least for some of them, they served in the military. And so you might have gone to Groton or Choate or Andover, Exeter, and those kinds of schools, but along comes World War I or World War II, and suddenly you’re in the barracks with all of America. And so they did not have the opportunity to become as insular as our elite is becoming, even more insular than the Protestant establishment, which is saying something. And so to me, when I think of how do you raise a better elite: First, I would hope our institution of education of all varieties would go back and teach what social leadership looks like; second, what social responsibility looks like; but third, would tell the truth—not in the way I’m about to say it, ’cause when I say it it’s laced with a bit of bitterness—which is stop being segregationists. Higher ed is a segregation system. And you tell people, “We’re blocking social mobility for your kids”; they will flip the tables. And so as a leadership class, there’s a lot of work that needs to be done on us, and I think there’s some dawning recognition that this needs to happen, but I’m not sure. Zakaria: No, I agree with everything you said. The question becomes: How do you fix it? I remember my first boss. I worked at Foreign Affairs; Jim Hoge, had gone to, I think, Exeter and Yale. But he then went— Brooks: Amazingly good-looking guy, by the way. Zakaria: Yes, yes. There was an Esquire magazine in which he and Robert Redford were both—and it was sort of: What do you do when you’re so good-looking that no one thinks you’re smart? Or something like that. And I have to confess— Brooks: Never been my problem. Zakaria: I thought to myself, I would kill to have that problem . But I think that the point he made to me, which I remember vividly, is he went from there, from Yale, to the Chicago Sun-Times as a cub reporter or an intern, and he said not only was he the only person on the entire news floor who had gone to Yale; there were only about 20 percent of them who had gone to college. Eighty percent of the reporters. And journalism was a much more mixed enterprise. Now it’s an entirely elite enterprise. It may not be high-paying, but it’s intellectually elite, and that creates a certain conformism and insularity. And I think that one of the challenges has got to be to figure out—I think we still, in the way we do sorting and education, we have not figured out how to find smart poor kids. Statistically, intelligence is sprinkled roughly equally throughout the entire population. What that means is we’re not searching hard enough for the smart poor kid who didn’t go through the hoops, who didn’t get that early jump in or didn’t have a great teacher, and maybe that person then needs a little remedial education, or maybe they need to go to summer school. But we are missing that because we need those people because it’s right; it’s fair; it’s just. But it’s also that energy is a different kind of energy. That drive is a different kind of drive, and I don’t think we’ve figured out how to do it. The other point I want to make about Plutarch is I think here I’m somewhat hopeful for an unusual reason. I think AI is going to be on almost everything an absolutely revolutionary phenomena, but think about it this way. I think since the Enlightenment, human beings have begun to think of themselves almost entirely as analytic machines. Before that, when we couldn’t understand something, we said, “God did it.” Why is there day and night? Well, the sun god moves his chariot across the sky, and that’s why you have day and night. And why do we have spring? Well, Persephone, the goddess of spring, wakes up. And then we started to apply our minds and reason and the scientific method to uncover the mysteries of the universe, and it was mind-blowing. We were able to understand all these things that we hadn’t been able to. AI is now going to take us back to a world where, to uncover the mysteries of the universe, we have to rely on another black box. It’s not called religion; it’s called AI. But the AI will explain things and solve things and do stuff that we just cannot do analytically. We are no longer the best analytic machine in the universe. And so then the question is: What do we do as human beings? Well, maybe we recover the older qualities of character and temperament and intellect that mattered, which is that we search for wisdom and judgment and courage and leadership and those qualities that inspire people. That’s what they built statues for thousands of years ago. It wasn’t the smartest kid in the class; it was the person who had courage, who could inspire, who did lead. So maybe, in a strange way, it will bring us back to that because we can’t pretend that we’re just going to be analytic machines because there’s going to be an actual machine that does it better. Brooks: I would just say the thing that to me matters most is desire and determination, and that if we were awarded that, we would have a much more democratic meritocracy. But the hopeful thing— Zakaria: And by the way, that’s one of the great things about America, and that gives me great hope because in every rich society, the challenges drive determination because you become rich. Sometimes when I talk to a bunch of bankers or, you know, rich people, I will sometimes say, “Now let me ask you a question. You guys are all incredibly talented, and you have extraordinary capabilities. But when you look at your children, do you think they have the same drive that you did?” And usually about 10 percent of the audience will put their hands up. Because at the end of the day, the children are reacting rationally to their circumstances. They’re growing up in enormous wealth, and it’s hard to have that. But immigrants do. And the fact that America still takes more legal immigrants than, for example, all of Europe put together every year, I think that is one of the things that makes sure that the United States remains forward-leaning, optimistic, driven. It has that culture of growth and aspiration because it’s very hard to force it, to tell people, “I know you’re rich, but pretend you’re poor.” That doesn’t work. You kind of actually have to be from the outside, trying to break in. Brooks: One of the things I think we agree upon is this is a moment of shaking loose a lot. Even before the midterms, you wrote a column on, and yeah, I’m going to read two sentences from you: “We are living in an age of anxiety, and that means people are unsure about their political allegiances.” Boy, did that turn out to be true. Everybody’s floating all over the place. Zakaria: Think about Hispanics moved 20 points in 2024 and then 20 points back in 2026. Brooks: So suddenly we’re in a period of flux, and not only a period of political flux; I think we’re in a period of moral flux. I think basically people took a look at MAGA, and they felt some sense of moral shame. I’ve always had a certain idea about America, is that we were vain; we were overconfident; we could be dumb and naive and crass, but we were not malevolent. And I’ve now thought, Okay, we’ve been malevolent . And so to me that gives us an opportunity really to turn a page and to reinvent the liberalism that you and I both believe in. So the question is: What part of liberalism do you lead? It’s not only a set of ideas; it’s a way of life. But what is the part that is most needing to be recovered or reemphasized, or something like that? Zakaria: So to me, the part I think that we have to get right, and we can get right, is we have created a highly unequal society. Partly the machinations of capitalism sometimes do that. There are some winner-take-all dynamics to, for example, technology industry, where everybody wants to use the same search engine that everybody else uses, so you get this winner-take-all phenomena. But a lot of it is also, frankly, corruption and structural advantages. Then there’s, of course, the massive inequality in wealth and the taxation system that, for example, taxes capital gains at a much lower rate than income, which probably makes no sense. So if we can fix all of that and create a more genuinely open, fair, level playing field, greater access for people, giving people the ability, in enormously rich countries, to not have to worry about very basic things like health care. I actually think that universal health care would be a very pro-growth policy because one of the things that happens when you have the kind of crazy system we have is people don’t leave their jobs for fear of losing health care. When I was at Newsweek , I had to do four sets of layoffs, and every person I laid off understood we were in this collapsing market for magazines, and so I didn’t want to do it. They knew that this was being forced on me, but every single one, every single person I laid off asked me, “Is there any way I can keep my health care for a year or two years because of my kids?” And I think if you made it so that everyone had it—you know, a basic level—I think it would create more entrepreneurship, more people willing to take risks. If you can fix all that, which I think is possible, you can renew the idea of the promise of a genuinely liberal society, where individuals are treated like individuals and have certain benefits but rights. The question I have for you is: If some of this right-wing populism, if some of this reaction, negative reaction, to a liberal society is cultural, is this sense of, What happened to that world of community and faith and belonging that I believed in?— we can’t just put Humpty Dumpty back together again; we can’t create a white Christian America again, whether or not that was as good or as stable even as people remember—so what do you do? Brooks: I’m pretty open to some radical left ideas. I don’t know about universal health care because I’m not sure how we make the transition, and I don’t know how we afford it. My radical part on the left would be some sort of basic insurance, so there’s security, whether it’s EITC, or an earned income tax credit, subsidies, some sort of health care. It can’t be crazy the way it is now. I worry about sapping the spirit of energy the way I believe Europe has. I would adopt some much bigger welfare state, but you gotta give me job growth and economic dynamism. And to me that’s regulations, but also—and this is the thing maybe we can close on, and I don’t know if America will ever believe in this again—but to me one of the greatest things about liberalism is pluralism. That America, like your family and my family, it was a crossroads nation. We attracted hungry immigrants, and they did great things. And there’s a book by a guy named Sir Peter Hall named [ Cities in Civilization ], and he looked at the most innovative places in world history, and they were all crossroads nations: Athens, Florence, Vienna, New York, Silicon Valley. And Hall writes, “People meet, people talk, people listen to each other’s music and each other’s words. They dance each other’s dances and take in each other’s thoughts. Sparks might be struck and something new comes out of the encounter.” That’s liberalism to me, and America’s so averse to diversity now all of a sudden. Maybe we can’t go back there, but I’ll give you your socialist welfare state if you give me free capitalism and a lot of economic and demographic diversity. Zakaria: So the challenge then is if you want that diversity—and I entirely agree with you. I mean, you look at any of the great societies in the world—you know, the Netherlands that I talk about in the book—that invented really modern liberalism, modern capitalism, incredibly diverse. They were willing to take in persecuted Protestants. They were willing to take in Jews. But it does cause people to feel like we are losing our common culture. We are losing our traditions. And that’s in some ways what’s happened here, and to me, that remains the central challenge. How do you create a society where you celebrate diversity? You encourage it; you want those people; you love the vitality, the spread; you love the kind of enriching and ennobling that takes place with those kind of encounters. But you do create anxiety. You do create a sense that people feel like, I don’t recognize my country anymore. This world is passing me by . And it’s fascinating that this reaction, this backlash, has been with us as long as liberalism has. And nobody has come up with an adequate solution to it. Because at the end of the day, the solution that is often tried, which is some kind of coercion or repression, not only doesn’t work, but it so runs counter to the spirit of liberalism. How do you resolve this dilemma? Brooks: A strong national narrative and strong symbols of America that unite us all. We need bigger White House ballrooms and maybe an arch near Reagan National. Fareed Zakaria, thank you so much for joining us on The Permanent Questions . Zakaria: David Brooks, such a pleasure. Brooks: One of the things I appreciate about Fareed is that he is a journalist. He has a weekly show on CNN, so he’s covering the news right up to the date. But as you heard, he has this background with Samuel Huntington, and he’s got a broader historical perspective, which came out especially in that last book, [ Age of Revolutions ]. And having someone who has a historical perspective on our current moment in one sense was sobering to me because he said we’ve been here before. There are these moments of great diversity, great change. People rebel. You get a backlash. But the problem is not so easy to put it back together. And I think if you were hopefully like, “Oh, we’re just turning the page on MAGA; we’re all going to move forward now,” I think you should not believe that. But the nice thing about him, which I found exciting, was that he did talk about how big the change is. We can’t go back to the things I’m sort of nostalgic for: some of the moral order, some of the way things used to be, the notion that marriage was sort of a natural thing that most people were going to be aiming for at some point in their life. That’s not all happening. And technology is technology, and AI is AI. And so what we have to do, I guess, as people who want to restore liberal democracies where people get to run their lives and do things like that, is we have to reenvision these systems for an entirely different era. And I think that’s a project that is not going to just take the removal of Donald Trump and MAGA, but will take a lot of thinking over maybe the next 15, 20 years. And so that’s a new age. But it does reinforce the idea to me that we are past peak populism, that at least in the United States, that era is over, and now we’re in the process of what is struggling to be born. Thanks so much for joining us at The Permanent Questions with Fareed Zakaria. The Permanent Questions is produced and edited by The Atlantic in partnership with Yale University. New episodes come out on Sundays. You can watch The Permanent Questions on The Atlantic ’s YouTube channel, on Spotify, Apple, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. See you next week.

items.title: The World the Telephone Made
items.description: High-tech gadgets proliferated almost as rapidly in Mark Twain’s time as they do in ours, and he prided himself on being an early adopter. So when Alexander Graham Bell’s new telephone company began to offer service in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1877, Twain signed up, boasting (incorrectly) that his was the first line “ever used in a private house in the world.” Shortly afterward, he did set a record, becoming “the first author to deploy the telephone in fiction, in a peculiar story for The Atlantic Monthly ,” James Gleick writes in The Telephone: A New History . The comedy of “ The Loves of Alonzo Fitz Clarence and Rosannah Ethelton ” comes mainly from its high-concept premise: The title characters fall in love, quarrel, reconcile, and get married entirely over the phone, without ever meeting in person. At the time the story appeared, in March 1878, very few Americans had actually seen a telephone, and Twain plays up the strangeness of the new technology. When we are first introduced to Alonzo, in his study in Eastport, Maine, he seems to be talking to himself, or to someone in the next room, before it’s revealed that he’s actually on the phone with his Aunt Susan in San Francisco. But although Twain found technology fascinating, he also knew that things—even things that do amazing things—don’t make for good stories. The only subject that human beings find enduringly interesting is one another, and Twain was remarkably prescient about how the telephone would challenge traditional terms of interaction. The lovers in Twain’s story are separated by thousands of miles, but the conversation between them is not at either end, nor is it somewhere in the middle; it is a meeting of minds that have escaped the body’s requirement of place. This raises questions that we’re still asking today, in the age of dating apps and OnlyFans. Can people be real to one another without physical presence? Can there be love without touch? “There was a feeble but frantic sound for some little time, as if wool-lipped, disembodied spirits were exchanging kisses,” Twain writes about his telephone lovers. Is that funny or nightmarish? Gleick’s great achievement as a science writer has been to show how complicated, abstract ideas end up changing the way we experience the world. In Chaos , he explored chaos theory, which used new mathematical tools to explain why weather and other complex systems are so unpredictable. In The Information , he showed how modern discoveries such as DNA and the computer involved new ways of thinking about data and communication. The Telephone , too, is the story of a scientific discovery. But it’s just as much the history of a business—the Bell System, a group of companies led by the American Telephone and Telegraph Company (AT&T) that became America’s most powerful and enduring monopoly. The book is also a wide-ranging cultural history, showing how the telephone changed people’s lives and how they tried to make sense of those changes. When Bell gave a public demonstration of his invention in Salem, Massachusetts, speaking with Thomas Watson 18 miles away, in Boston, “it seemed as if an electric thrill went through the audience,” he remembered. “They recognized for the first time—what was meant by the ‘Telephone.’ ” But what did it mean, exactly? That is where novelists like Twain came in—along with playwrights, psychologists, social scientists, and legions of pundits in what Gleick calls the “Telephone Century.” Like artificial intelligence today, the telephone was an obviously momentous new technology that everyone had heard about and no one fully understood. If the parallel holds, we won’t know how AI is going to change the world until after it happens, because early predictions about how people would use the telephone turned out to be wildly off base. A New York Times article imagined it as a way to listen to sermons without having to go to church, joking that soon houses for rent would offer Baptist preachers “laid on in every room,” like hot and cold water. In France, the Théâtrophone service allowed subscribers (including Marcel Proust) to listen to live opera performances over the phone. In both cases, the telephone was viewed as a one-way delivery system. But its power would lie in being a network—literally, a web of metal cables spanning continents and oceans, which allowed any two people, anywhere in the world, to have a back-and-forth exchange. Not even Bell knew at first exactly what he was inventing. The initial goal of his research wasn’t to transmit the human voice, but to increase the carrying capacity of existing telegraph lines by sending multiple messages simultaneously at different pitches. In the course of his experiments with vibrating steel reeds, he discovered the principle that made the telephone possible: Sound and electricity speak the same language. Sound travels through the air in waves of pressure, and electromagnetic force also takes the form of a wave. The telephone was a tool for translating between the two kinds of waves. A small magnet, vibrating in response to a speaking voice, would generate an electrical current, which could be sent down a wire and reconverted into sound at the other end. Bell wasn’t the only person to make this discovery. Philipp Reis had built a device he called das Telephon in Germany in 1861, and Elisha Gray, an American inventor, was so close on Bell’s heels that both men’s applications reached the U.S. Patent Office on the same day. Bell was awarded the patent, as well as the chance to go down in history as the inventor of the telephone, mainly because his well-connected Washington lawyer bribed the patent examiner with $100 and a gold watch. Making the new invention useful would be a lot more expensive. As Gleick observes, other Industrial Age enterprises benefited from economies of scale. The more automobiles you make, the cheaper manufacturing each one becomes. With the telephone, the calculation was reversed: The bigger the network, the greater the cost per call, given how many lines and switchboards were required to put all the calls through. Raising capital from ultrarich investors became crucial. Originally Bell was one of four partners in the company that bore his name. Within three years, he had been reduced to one of 540 shareholders and ceased to play any real role. At first, independent telephone companies tried to challenge the Bell System, in business and in court. Some enterprising farmers even turned their barbed-wire fences into telephone lines by running electric current through them. But Bell’s patents gave AT&T an unbeatable head start, and it ruthlessly maintained its advantage for more than a century. In the 1920s, for instance, a small company called Hush-a-Phone started to sell a cheap plastic device that attached to the mouthpiece of a telephone; talking into it would make your desk phone “private as a booth.” But AT&T prohibited customers from using any third-party equipment, and “when company repair personnel saw a Hush-a-Phone in a customer’s home, they threatened to disconnect service altogether,” Gleick writes. Not until the case reached a federal appeals court, in 1956, did the company finally win the right to sell its $10 product. An antitrust suit led to the breakup of AT&T in 1984. By then, the telephone was so ubiquitous that its effect on modern life could hardly be grasped. Over a century, the meaning of distance had changed: The other side of the country, or the planet, didn’t seem so far away when you could communicate across it instantly, instead of waiting weeks to exchange letters. Privacy had become more accessible—teenagers could take the phone into their room, or a closet, and talk without a chaperone. But it was also more vulnerable. You couldn’t be sure that you weren’t being eavesdropped on—in the early days, by an operator or by a neighbor on a party line; later on, by someone picking up an extension or, if you were important enough, by a government wiretapper. FPG / Getty Operating switchboards came to be seen as women’s work—mainly because women were thought to be better than young men at sitting still and could be paid less. The telephone helped bring women into the public sphere, too, by creating a new kind of job. “As if by heavenly decree,” Gleick writes, “a consensus formed that operating a switchboard was women’s work,” and that “only women were suited to it”—mainly because they were better than young men at sitting still and could be paid lower wages. Even so, the job offered many women a path to personal independence and professional respect. When the U.S. Army needed skilled telephone operators during World War I, it had no choice but to hire women, although by law they couldn’t enlist in the military. In 1918, the 33 women of Telephone Unit No. 1 shipped out for France, where they “ate army food and slept in army barracks,” and wore their own armbands, embroidered with “black telephone transmitters and yellow streaks of lightning.” After that war, and even more so after World War II, women found new telephone-related jobs in offices as receptionists and secretaries. But switchboard operators were doomed by their own success. America’s telephone network was expanding so fast that there weren’t enough women to keep up. Around 1910, AT&T’s chief engineer estimated that by 1930, at least a quarter of New York City’s population would be needed just to run its switchboards. The company had to find a way to automate the process of making phone calls. The solution turned out to be the rotary dial, which allowed callers to enter the phone number they wanted to reach instead of telling it to an operator. Gleick shows that each major advance in telephone technology followed the same pattern: Science would rise to the demands of business. Technical challenges, such as signal amplification for long-distance calls, seemed insurmountable until they were solved. Then they were taken for granted. Harold M. Lambert / Getty How to dial a rotary phone. This dynamic is familiar in our own time too. Yesterday’s miracle becomes today’s necessity and tomorrow’s antique. The rotary dial was so cutting-edge in the 1920s that AT&T worried that customers wouldn’t be able to use it. New phones came printed with instructions: “Remove receiver. Put finger in hole over first figure wanted. Turn to stop and let go.” Today, you’d need to give the same explanation to people under 30, who have grown up in a world of touch screens. Among other things, The Telephone is an almanac of this kind of extinct knowledge. Depending on how old you are, you’ll feel nostalgic about different phases of telephone history: Remember dial tones? The Yellow Pages? Pay phones? Calling for the time? Now the telephone itself is history. By collective agreement, we refer to the devices in our hands at every waking moment as phones—maybe iPhones or cellphones, but never telephones. Phones can do a million things that telephones never dreamed of, while the one thing telephones did is starting to feel unnecessary, even impolite. When a phone rings—an anachronism; phones don’t ring, they vibrate or light up or play a tune—it’s more likely to be a scammer or a salesperson than a friend. If you really want to communicate with someone, you send a text or set up a Zoom call. Fittingly, Gleick ends his book with a visit to a disconnected telephone booth in Japan, which a local man has turned into a shrine of sorts—a place to think about the absent and the dead, who have no phone number. Duncan Raban / Popperfoto / Getty A Motorola DynaTAC 8000x, the first commercial mobile phone, circa 1985. Even if we’ve moved beyond telephones, however, we still inhabit the strange new dimension they opened up. The telephone gave humanity its first experience of what we now call the virtual—a kind of reality that is divorced from presence. By translating the human voice into a signal transmitted through a wire, the telephone gave it the reach of electricity and the abstractness of data. At first, telephone users experienced this as a magic power—“this admirable magic that needs only a few seconds to bring before us, unseen but present, the person to whom we wish to speak,” as Proust described it. What Bell did not foresee is that once human beings got a taste of this freedom, having a body and being in a place began to feel burdensome, a concession to the limitations of the physical world. Ever since, the information-technology revolution that began in the 1870s with the telephone and phonograph has been steadily lightening that burden. Radio, television, movies, and the internet have claimed an ever larger share of our attention for people and things not actually there . AI is completing the emancipation from reality that the telephone began. When you had a conversation on the phone, you could at least be sure that the voice on the other end of the line belonged to a real person. Today we are surrounded by sounds and images that never corresponded to anything real—lifelike photos of people who were never born, intimate conversations with machines that can’t think or feel. The great irony of the telephone is that a device born as a tool of communication, bringing people together across distances, has evolved into our most effective tool of solipsism. No long-distance call can bridge the space between two people absorbed in their phones, even when they’re sitting side by side. This article appears in the January 2027 print edition with the headline “The World the Telephone Made.”

items.title: Algérie : le gouvernement débloque près de 1,7 milliard de dollars pour le développement ferroviaire
items.description: L'Algerie a lance des projets ferroviaires d'envergure dans plusieurs parties du pays. Afin de se donner les moyens de mener ces ambitions, deux decrets presidentiels, publies au Journal officiel sous les numeros 79 et 80, ont autorise le deblocage d'un total de plus de 238 milliards de dinars (soit pres de 1,7 milliard de dollars), consacres quasi exclusivement au developpement des infrastructures ferroviaires et aux transports guides. Le premier decret, datant du 18 octobre dernier, a accorde un credit de 170 milliards de dinars (plus de 1,2 milliard de dollars) au titre de l'exercice budgetaire 2026. Quatre jours plus tard, au 22 octobre, un second texte a consenti une rallonge de 68,26 milliards de dinars (pres de 500 millions de dollars), au profit du programme « Infrastructures ferroviaires et transports guides », au sous-programme « Developpement des infrastructures ferroviaires » et au titre 3 « Depenses d'investissement » du portefeuille de programmes du ministere des Travaux publics et des Infrastructures de base, selon le decret presidentiel. Les grands projets strategiques de voies ferrees Par la securisation des financements, le gouvernement algerien veut assurer sa feuille de route qui privilegie l'efficacite et le maillage intelligent du territoire afin de relier directement les bassins industriels et les gisements miniers aux ports au nord du pays, et ce, pour fluidifier le fret et alleger durablement la facture logistique nationale. Dans ce contexte, une ligne ferroviaire de 950 kilometres reliant le gisement de minerai de fer de Gara Djebilet a Bechar a deja ete inauguree le 1ᵉʳ fevrier dernier par le president de la Republique, Abdelmadjid Tebboune. Un projet ambitieux de chemin de fer de plus de 2 000 kilometres, reliant Alger a Tamanrasset, a deja ete realise et a livre 308 kilometres de rails. La fin des travaux et la mise en service sont prevues pour 2028 par le gouvernement avec un investissement evalue a environ 14,6 milliards de dollars. Sur le flanc oriental, le projet de la ligne miniere de l'Est progresse vers l'achevement de ce corridor strategique, long de 425 kilometres, qui va relier le gisement de phosphate de Bled El Hadba, dans la wilaya de Tebessa, au port d'Annaba. Les autorites algeriennes prevoient une entree en exploitation de cette ligne des le premier trimestre 2027. Parallelement a ces projets, le maillage ferroviaire existant est modernise activement, a l'instar du chantier de la desserte Tiaret-Tissemsilt dans les Hauts-Plateaux, de la mise a niveau de l'axe nord-ouest ou encore du raccordement des ports et des nouvelles. Une ambition de 15 000 kilometres de rails a l'horizon 2030 L'orientation actuelle du gouvernement algerien vers l'investissement massif en infrastructure ferroviaire s'inscrit dans le cadre d'une ambition bien plus grande portant les 5 700 kilometres de rails exploites actuellement a 15 000 kilometres a l'horizon 2030. L'enjeu pour l'etat est de fluidifier les echanges entre les zones industrielles et minieres et les ports en reduisant les coûts logistiques, mais aussi de respecter les echeances fixees pour ces projets ferroviaires avant le coup d'envoi des nouveaux cycles d'investissements dans divers secteurs economiques prevus pour 2028.

items.title: GTEC suspends new PhD admissions pending nationwide review of doctoral programmes
items.description: The Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC) has suspended new admissions into PhD programmes across tertiary institutions as it undertakes a nationwide audit of doctoral training. Director-General of GTEC, Professor Abdullah Jinapor, said the exercise would assess the accreditation status of programmes, student enrolment, qualifications of supervisors, research facilities, completion rates and the conduct of thesis examinations. Speaking at the University of Mines and Technology’s (UMaT) 19th Congregation in Tarkwa, he said the review was aimed at protecting the quality and credibility of doctoral qualifications awarded by Ghanaian institutions. “Its purpose is not to punish; it is to protect the credibility of the Ghanaian doctorate, so that a PhD earned in Ghana commands respect at home and abroad,” he said. Professor Jinapor expressed concern about what he described as excessive admissions into some doctoral programmes, questioning whether the institutions had enough qualified supervisors and resources to provide adequate academic support. He cited an institution that had admitted more than 250 PhD students, including 52 into a single programme, as an example of the concerns surrounding enrolment and supervision. He warned that institutions running doctoral programmes primarily for financial gain risk having them suspended. “Those that are doing well, like UMaT, we’ll allow you to. But those that are producing them for the sake of money, we are going to stop it. So, in the meantime, GTEC, unfortunately, is putting a freeze on the acceptance of new PhD applications until we are done with this exercise,” he said. Meanwhile, Professor Jinapor has dismissed claims that GTEC is recruiting lecturers for universities, insisting that the responsibility rests with the individual institutions. He explained that the Commission was facilitating access to qualified PhD holders to help universities address academic staffing shortages. He disclosed that GTEC had identified 97 PhD holders through the initiative, some of whom had expressed interest in taking up academic positions. “GTEC does not recruit, appoint or post lecturers to any institution. Recruitment remains the responsibility of each institution under its own Act, statutes and appointment procedures. And that autonomy remains fully intact,” he said. Professor Jinapor urged the University Teachers Association of Ghana (UTAG) and university authorities to recognise the Commission’s role in maintaining academic standards while respecting the autonomy of tertiary institutions.

items.title: Viandes rouges : les autorités renforcent les contrôles dans les boucheries de Casablanca
items.description: Les autorités locales de la ville de Casablanca ont lancé une campagne de contrôle et de sensibilisation ciblant les boucheries, afin d'inciter les professionnels à respecter l'obligation d'afficher les prix des viandes mises en vente et d'en préciser la provenance. Cette initiative vise à renforcer la transparence des transactions commerciales et à préserver le pouvoir d'achat des consommateurs. Ces opérations s'inscrivent dans le cadre de la mise en œuvre des directives visant à mieux encadrer les marchés de vente des viandes rouges et à permettre aux consommateurs de disposer d'informations claires sur la nature des viandes proposées, qu'elles soient produites localement ou importées, ainsi que sur leurs prix avant tout achat. Selon les informations disponibles, les autorités compétentes ont entamé des tournées de terrain, au cours desquelles elles ont pris contact avec les propriétaires de boucheries pour les sensibiliser à la nécessité d'afficher des listes claires indiquant les prix des différentes catégories de viandes ainsi que leur provenance. L'objectif est de permettre aux citoyens de distinguer les produits proposés et de faire leurs choix d'achat sur la base d'informations précises. La campagne ne se limite pas à Casablanca. Les autorités d'Ouled Ahmed, dans la province de Nouaceur, ont également lancé des opérations de contrôle des viandes dans le cadre de la sécurité sanitaire des aliments. Ces interventions portent notamment sur la vérification de leur qualité et la sensibilisation des bouchers à l'obligation d'afficher les prix et l'origine des produits commercialisés. Auparavant, les autorités gouvernementales avaient adressé une circulaire portant sur la nécessité d'afficher les prix des viandes et de distinguer clairement les viandes locales des viandes importées. Cette démarche s'inscrit dans une volonté de renforcer les règles de transparence et de mettre fin à toute pratique susceptible d'induire le consommateur en erreur ou de le priver de son droit à connaître la nature du produit qu'il achète. Pour les professionnels du secteur des viandes rouges, l'obligation faite aux boucheries d'afficher les prix et de préciser la provenance des viandes devrait contribuer à mieux organiser les opérations de vente et à renforcer la confiance entre les bouchers et les consommateurs. The post Viandes rouges : les autorités renforcent les contrôles dans les boucheries de Casablanca appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Some roads reopen, multiple still closed as political parties hold demonstration, rally in Karachi
items.description: Multiple roads were closed in Karachi as the Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) staged a demonstration in the city and the Jeay Sindh Rehbar Committee (JSRC) — a conglomerate of four Sindhi nationalist groups — held a rally on Sunday. However, two of the closed routes have now been reopened as the JUI-F’s main demonstration at Guru Mandir has ended. Routes that remain closed Both sides of Deen Mohammad Wafai Road have been closed to traffic and vehicles are being diverted from MR Kiani Chowrangi towards Thana Gali and from Fawara Chowk towards Zainab Market The stretch of Sharea Faisal that leads to Drigh Road and Karsaz is also closed to traffic. Commuters coming from the airport are being diverted via Rashid Minhas Bridge towards Millennium Mall The stretch of the city’s main artery from Avari Towers towards FTC is also closed for traffic, and vehicles are being diverted from Avari Towers towards Fatima Jinnah Road and Sindh Club Reopened roads The route from Askari 4 to Drigh Road has been reopened for traffic The route from Guru Mandir towards Jamshed Road has also been reopened The alerts for road closures had cited “security” as the reason, except for the blockade of the route between Guru Mandir and Jamshed Road. The alert for this closure said the road had been blocked due to a planned demonstration by the JUI-F. The JUI-F had said in a statement that while its main demonstration would be held at Guru Mandir, protests would also be held at its headquarters, press clubs and other locations across Sindh against the “violation of the sanctity of JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s residence, the ongoing smear campaign against him, and the conspiracy to divide Sindh”. Meanwhile, the JSRC had announced a rally to protest the proposal to create new provinces and divide Sindh. A four-member PPP committee began efforts on Friday to persuade nationalist parties to postpone their planned rallies in Karachi, but failed to do so. Over the past few months, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has whipped up a political storm since he called for the formation of new administrative units in the country, saying the current “system” of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”. The PPP, which is in power in Sindh, has been clear in its stance against carving out any new federating units in the province but has been calling for the creation of a South Punjab province. The Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan, which is an ally of the ruling PML-N along with the PPP in the Centre and in opposition in Sindh, has been insisting on the creation of new provinces and has thrown its weight behind the proposal to hold a referendum on the matter.

items.title: Search for Indonesia factory fire missing to resume Monday, police remove 24 body bags
items.description: Indonesian police removed 24 body bags from a factory destroyed by fire in Java on Sunday as firefighters battled remaining hotspots a day after the blaze tore through the building and a search for dozens of missing workers was suspended overnight. Metro TV footage showed distraught family members weeping outside the factory as they waited for news of relatives feared to have been caught in the blaze. Search operations are scheduled to resume on Monday morning, Hendra Kurniawan, the police chief of Indonesia’s Banten province, told Metro TV . Steven Erwin Wijaya, the CEO of the factory, said at a press conference that around 300 people were present for Saturday’s shift. In a later statement, the factory said that 24 of the 65 workers involved had returned home, 4 were receiving medical treatment, 29 remained missing and the whereabouts of another 8 had yet to be confirmed. At the same press conference, Wahyu Hidayati, a police disaster victim identification official, said the intensity of the fire had rendered the recovered victims unidentifiable via visual inspection, prompting efforts to collect DNA samples from relatives and the personal belongings of the missing workers, a process that could take two to three weeks. The number of dead was not immediately clear, with police saying that one body bag could contain parts of more than one person. Authorities said the cause of the fire was being investigated. The fire broke out on Saturday evening at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia candy factory in Cikande, in the Serang regency. Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex. Photos and videos shared by rescuers also showed officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims, with small fires still burning in some spots. Relatives of the missing victims flocked near the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones, footage aired by local broadcasters showed. Earlier, search teams were combing sections of the damaged building where victims were believed to be trapped, while parts of the building remained at risk of collapse, an official said. The factory is part of Indonesia’s United Family Food company, founded in 1981, according to its website. It produces consumer goods across Indonesia, employs about 5,000 people and operates from its national headquarters and four international offices, serving a market of more than 250 million consumers.

items.title: 2027: Atiku’s ally dismisses Fubara’s 3m votes pledge to Tinubu
items.description: …Insists Rivers is nobody’s political inheritance, says APC must be punished for emergency rule By Daniel Abia PORT HARCOURT — A chieftain of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and close ally of its presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, Chief Eze Chukwuemeka Eze, has dismissed Governor Siminalayi Fubara’s pledge to deliver three million votes for President Bola Tinubu in the 2027 general election. Eze described the governor’s assurance as an unrealistic political projection, insisting that Rivers State was not the political inheritance of any individual or group. Fubara had, on November 7, during a Rainbow Coalition/APC presidential rally in Port Harcourt, assured Tinubu that the people of Rivers would deliver at least three million votes for him in the January 2027 presidential election. Reacting to the pledge in a statement issued in Port Harcourt at the weekend, Eze described it as an “audacious exercise in political delusion, electoral deception and monumental grandstanding”. He argued that the projection was unattainable and disconnected from the prevailing political realities in the state, alleging that the governor made the promise to massage the President’s ego and create an impression of widespread political acceptance. The ADC chieftain said Tinubu’s reliance on political assurances from Fubara and the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, showed a misunderstanding of the political consciousness of Rivers people and their grievances over the political crisis that engulfed the state. Eze recalled the declaration of a state of emergency in Rivers, the suspension of the governor, his deputy and members of the State House of Assembly, insisting that the people had neither forgotten nor forgiven the circumstances surrounding the intervention. He said Rivers people were politically enlightened enough to distinguish genuine leadership from political manoeuvring and would not surrender their electoral choices to intimidation, patronage or political inducements. “It is rather amusing that President Tinubu appears to have mistaken political silence for political acquiescence and the orchestrated jubilation at Adokiye Amiesimaka Stadium for an irrevocable endorsement of his administration,” he said. Eze also cautioned against interpreting the crowd at the APC rally as an indication of the President’s electoral strength in the state. “Let nobody deceive the President with the political theatrics of Nyesom Wike, Governor Siminalayi Fubara and their respective political establishments. “The crowd assembled at the stadium, regardless of its numerical appearance, cannot be substituted for the electorate. A rented or politically mobilised crowd, no matter how imposing, does not constitute an electoral mandate,” he said. He further predicted that Tinubu would struggle to secure 100,000 genuine votes in Rivers in 2027, adding that even such a figure would not necessarily amount to an endorsement of his administration. The ADC chieftain also accused the President and his political associates of assuming that they could influence the judiciary, security agencies and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to determine the outcome of the 2027 elections. He warned that such assumptions could undermine democracy, stressing that the institutions were established by the Constitution and should not serve the interests of any political party or administration. Eze said the Rivers political crisis had exposed the dangers of political arrogance, executive overreach and the subordination of constitutional democracy to personal political interests. He added that Nigerians facing economic hardship and what he described as failed governance would use the ballot box to express their dissatisfaction and determine the country’s political future. The ADC chieftain insisted that Rivers State was not the political property of any individual, warning that neither political alliances nor the influence of power brokers could guarantee electoral support. He said the 2027 elections would ultimately be determined by voters, not political promises, rallies or claims of control over the electorate.
