items.title: La campaña eleva el drama en la recta final: “¡A por ellos!”. “¡No pasarán!”
items.description: La plaza de toros de Valencia, completamente llena, espera el momento cumbre del mitin: la salida de su líder, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, más crecido que nunca tras el debate del jueves. Pero antes de verlo en persona, los militantes lo miran en dibujos animados. En la pantalla gigante aparece un vídeo de anime: Sánchez es un malvado monstruo enorm e, de capa negra y ojos rojos, que lanza rayos del mismo color y domina con ellos a miles de ciudadanos también con ojos enrojecidos. Entonces llega Feijóo como un superhéroe que lanza rayos azules y vence a Sánchez para salvar al pueblo. El público aplaude enfervorecido. Poco después sale el líder del PP, el real, y avisa: “no os fieis de nada. Son capaces de todo, y heridos son todavía más peligrosos”. Y ahí la plaza de toros entera, de forma espontánea y por primera vez en un mitin del PP, canta “¡A por ellos, oé! ¡A por ellos, oé!”, mientras Feijóo sonríe. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Doce horas en campaña con Pedro Sánchez: “La última vez que la ultraderecha gobernó no había democracia”
items.description: Pedro Sánchez llega caminando bajo los cedros y cipreses que separan el palacete de la Moncloa, residencia del presidente del Gobierno desde 1977, del edificio donde le aguardan sus ministros. Viene solo, sin India ni Turka , las dos perras de agua que a veces le acompañan en sus paseos, y con la prensa leída y un café en el cuerpo, lo único que suele tomar durante su ayuno entre cenas y comidas. Son poco más de las 9.00, apenas han pasado 10 horas de su debate con Alberto Núñez Feijóo . En redes, sondeos y medios le dan por derrotado. Le critican desde el aire ausente al color del traje. Otra cosa es La Moncloa. Los ministros socialistas le recibirán con un aplauso. Y el propio protagonista se considera vencedor. Por la tarde dirá a EL PAÍS que se impuso en los tres objetivos que perseguía: la buena política contra la mala educación, los datos verdaderos contra los bulos y el contraste en el proyecto de país. “Puede que a los más cafeteros y a la prensa, que quiere más mambo, les parezca que no ha golpeado donde debería, pero el objetivo era hacer un ejercicio de cirugía y apelar al votante más moderado para que vea que la polarización existe, pero es asimétrica”, reflexiona Diego Rubio, su jefe de gabinete, sentado en una sala colindante a la del consejo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La revancha de Feijóo consigo mismo
items.description: Más que una revancha contra Pedro Sánchez, l a campaña del PP para las elecciones del 29 de noviembre parece una revancha de Alberto Núñez Feijóo consigo mismo . El candidato del PP está corrigiendo algunas de las debilidades que lastraron su posibilidad de llegar a La Moncloa hace tres años. Si en 2023 un Feijóo más inseguro evitó las entrevistas difíciles, dejó la silla vacía en el segundo debate electoral y cometió errores no forzados, el de ahora, más confiado, está yendo a todos los foros y debates y ha conseguido alcanzar el ecuador de la campaña sin tropiezos graves ni sobresaltos. Aunque todavía falta la semana decisiva hasta el 29-N, con pruebas muy importantes como el debate a cuatro y la entrevista en TVE, la sensación en el PP es que Feijóo no compite tanto contra Sánchez como contra la versión de sí mismo que dejó escapar la oportunidad en las últimas elecciones . Seguir leyendo

items.title: ¿Quiénes son los indecisos? En busca del dubitativo voto de izquierdas
items.description: Dos amigas de 20 años charlan frente a la playa de Calpe, una localidad costera a 60 kilómetros de Alicante. Hablan animadamente de sus cosas: de amigos, del trabajo o de la relación con sus padres. Lo tienen todo claro hasta que sale el tema de las elecciones y de votar. Y ahí sí, entran las dudas. Seguir leyendo Metodología Para que las cifras de indecisos sean consistentes se han utilizado los datos de las siguientes encuestas de 40dB. en 2026: el sondeo ‘flash’ de octubre, el barómetro preelectoral de noviembre, y el ‘tracking’ completo hasta el 20 de noviembre. En total, se han agrupado 7.800 entrevistas, reponderadas para que cada estudio tenga el mismo peso. Se han considerado indecisos los encuestados que ante la pregunta sobre intención de voto responden “No lo sé” y “Prefiero no contestar”. El voto en 2023 es el recuerdo declarado por el entrevistado, y “Otros” agrupa al resto de partidos. El ancho de cada partido del gráfico de la introducción corresponde a su peso en el voto válido de 2023, no al recuerdo de voto de la muestra. Lo mismo se aplica para los mapas de indecisos por partido y CCAA: el tamaño de los cuadrados es proporcional al peso del voto válido en los resultados de 2023, no del peso de la muestra.

items.title: Gabriel Rufián: “Más que fascismo hay hijoputismo; la maldad está de moda”
items.description: Es el político mejor valorado de España según el CIS, pero también uno de los que ha dejado a más personas con la miel en los labios las últimas semanas. Gabriel Rufián (Santa Coloma de Gramenet, Barcelona, 1982) encabeza la candidatura de Esquerra Republicana al Congreso después de no haber cuajado su apuesta por un frente de partidos a la izquierda del PSOE . No esconde que quiere que el PSOE vuelva a gobernar, pero lo quiere tener “sometido” o “tutelado” para evitar despistes hacia la derecha. Muy crítico con muchos medios de comunicación, su punto fuerte es la comunicación directa con sus potenciales votantes a través de las redes sociales. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Rosendo rompe ocho años de silencio: “Toda mi vida ha sido una pelea constante conmigo mismo”
items.description: Ahí está, conservando sus costumbres: los vaqueros, la melena (ya blanca y recogida en forma de coleta), el paquete de tabaco, su cara de buena persona. Y en Carabanchel, su barrio. La cita con EL PAÍS transcurre en una cafetería de ese distrito madrileño, donde sigue viviendo, aunque también pasa temporadas en el pequeño pueblo burgalés de Esther, su pareja, con la que se casó allá por 1977. Ocho años sin noticias del rockero español más carismático. En diciembre de 2018 se retiró de los conciertos y solo asomó levemente en 2022, invitado en el directo del 40 aniversario del disco Rock & Ríos para interpretar su himno Maneras de vivir. “Fue tremendo. Miguel [Ríos], que me saca diez años, estaba como una rosa después de dos horas de recital y yo salí cuatro minutos y acabé con un sofocón que no veas”, se ríe. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Alana S. Portero: “Veré los resultados con amigos y unos blísters de Lexatín”
items.description: En el bajo de 35 metros del barrio obrero de San Blas donde se crio Alana S. Portero, “se hablaba de política incluso cuando no se hablaba”: “Era inevitable, la política nos atravesaba… con las dificultades para llegar a fin de mes, con cómo estaba el barrio, con lo que les pasaba a nuestros vecinos. No había manera de no pensar en clave política”. Con 48 años, la autora madrileña del superventas La mala costumbre y la recién publicada Cosamala —que el 29N irá a votar con sus padres y luego comerán juntos—, sigue hablando de política, cuando escribe, da conferencias o se toma el cuarto café de la mañana. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Una mala noche
items.description: Volvía a casa después del concierto de Vetusta Morla, volvía como levitando por haber escuchado el clamor de esa multitud que coreaba viejas canciones y por esos brazos que se alzaron al cielo cuando Pucho, el vocalista, en representación del grupo, pidió a quien quisiera escuchar que hubiera un pacto para salvarnos de la fiereza del cambio climático, cuando luego nombró a la enseñanza pública, a la que en Madrid se le está dando con la puerta en las narices en la peor muestra de desconsideración que se haya visto jamás, cuando clamó por una vivienda digna y cuando, universalizando su discurso, arrancó una de sus canciones con un ¡Palestina libre!, que fue coreado por la multitud. Volvía tarde para ver el debate en su totalidad, pero alegre por presenciar a un público entusiasta que aplaudió tanto el arte como el compromiso, no tan común en un universo, el del pop, en el que a menudo se teme incomodar. Cuando ya en casa me incorporé a la discusión de los líderes tuve la sensación más extraña experimentada en esta campaña ya de por sí extravagante e indefinible. Un Sánchez desinflado, como ausente, respondía con tibieza a un taimado Feijóo que, valiéndose del ataque sin tregua, sin dejar respirar al adversario y algo descontrolado por parte de la moderadora, hacía gala de un supuesto pasado de espléndido gestor sin que su oponente le recordara sus muy discutibles “gestiones” en la la Xunta, algo que los gallegos conocen bien. ¿Los asesores asesoran? Todo el clamor que me había ensanchado el ánimo, esa jubilosa sensación de que hay ciudadanos dispuestos a luchar por una vida mejor, se esfumó, porque quien debía defenderlo con vehemencia se quedó como empanado. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Cayetana y el borrado de las mujeres
items.description: Esta semana, Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo explicó que nuestro país necesita “inmigración que trabaje mientras los españoles se ponen a tener bebés”. Ese mismo día, cinco países europeos acordaban impulsar un centro de deportación en Ruanda, iniciativa que Xavier García Albiol calificó de “fantástica”. No era una ocurrencia aislada, el programa del PP se compromete a impulsar centros de retorno en terceros países. Pero hay más. Parecería que no tiene nada que ver con todo esto, pero ese programa, llamado de “Reconstrucción nacional”, propone que el concebido no nacido compute para determinar las ayudas y beneficios a las familias. Vistas juntas, estas propuestas dibujan un modelo social donde la pertenencia empieza en el vientre de la mujer y su cuerpo se convierte en el lugar donde el Estado reconoce a sus miembros. Reproducción, pertenencia y utilidad se piensan juntas para el futuro de la comunidad, y por eso hay que calcular cuántos extranjeros (y extranjeras) hacen falta, y establecer mecanismos para expulsar a quienes dejen de servir. Seguir leyendo

items.description: El nombre es un regalo que se recibe al nacer y una de las huellas que quedan atrás al morir. Es “un rostro, una voz, una historia”, describe desde Alemania la activista afgana Lalah Osmany. En Afganistán, es también una de las pocas cosas que los talibanes aún no les han arrebatado a las mujeres desde su retorno al poder en 2021. Quién sabe por cuánto tiempo, porque una orden de los fundamentalistas en la provincia de Balj (norte) acaba de prohibir escribir el nombre de las afganas en los documentos oficiales, incluido en las recetas e historiales médicos, según confirman varias mujeres a este diario. items.title: Anatomía de Núcleo Nacional: los nazis que planeaban un alzamiento armado
items.description: El pasado 7 de octubre, un miembro de Núcleo Nacional expuso a su cúpula un dilema: “No podemos usar las mismas tácticas que en 1930. Los judíos han aprendido”. El neonazi pedía un giro de guion para asaltar el poder. Despojarse de la pátina antisemita, el combustible que alimentó el genocidio de seis millones de personas durante el Holocausto. Ante la sugerencia, la dirección de la milicia reaccionó como un resorte. “A Adolf Hitler le ofrecieron pactar muchas veces, pero no quiso”, zanjó la ideóloga, Isabel Peralta , que recordó al descarriado una línea roja: “La cuestión judía es la cuestión judía”. items.title: El enigma del palacio de Cuqui Fierro, la casa fantasma en la que vivió una de las mujeres más extravagantes de España
items.description: “La señora no está”, dice el guardés de la casa-palacio en el número 6 de la plaza del Marqués de Salamanca. El vigilante mira con desconfianza y mantiene la puerta de servicio entornada para no enseñar ni un centímetro de los casi 1.700 metros cuadrados de esta mansión privada en plena Milla de Oro de Madrid. La señora es Florentina Fierro Viña de Torróntegui, de 94 años, pilar de la alta sociedad capitalina desde hace más de seis décadas. Las mujeres de su clase suelen llevar apellidos larguísimos y nombres de dos sílabas: Tita, Totó, Piru, Fina, Mimi… A Florentina siempre la han llamado Cuqui. Hace unos años, la Real Academia aceptó “cuqui”, variante de “cuco”, con el sentido de “pulido, mono”. “La RAE permite el uso de la palabra ‘cuqui’ a los hablantes que ganen más de 10.000 euros al mes”, bromeó entonces el diario satírico El Mundo Today . items.title: Sánchez saca los pasos prohibidos del PSOE
items.description: Anuncia Salvados para este domingo una entrevista con Pedro Sánchez en La Sexta en el mismo bar en el que, un mes después de su defenestración en el PSOE, presentó los principios fundamentales de la narrativa de su primera resurrección. Se había equivocado llamando populista a Podemos, el PSOE estaba en tierra de nadie, existía una confabulación empresarial y mediática para impedir un Gobierno de izquierdas; y España era una “nación de naciones” y, como tal, tenía que ser considerada Cataluña en la Constitución. Un Sánchez desencadenado que provocó un terremoto en las filas socialistas y desconcertó a sus poderes de siempre: “Ha cavado su tumba”, sentenció aquella noche un prohombre que, como la gran mayoría de la cúpula de entonces, no supo ver la revolución que estaba por llegar. items.title: Forensic evidence points to servant in Hina Javaid murder as probe clears husband
items.description: • After nearly three-month delay, police submit charge sheet in high-profile murder case • According to the DNA analysis report, Hina Javaid was reportedly sexually assaulted after being murdered by her domestic servant RAWALPINDI: Rawalpindi police have completed their investigation into the high-profile murder of digital media executive Hina Javaid, who was found dead with signs of torture and strangulation at her husband’s apartment in Lal Kurti in August. The police submitted the challan to the court after about three months. The development was disclosed by newly appointed City Police Officer (CPO) Rawalpindi Sardar Ghias Gul during his first interaction with media persons on Saturday. Hina Javaid was murdered on August 20, 2026, at her husband’s house, and her domestic servant has been identified as the main suspect in the case following a forensic DNA match and a report by a high-level inquiry committee. Hina Javaid’s husband and his father have been cleared of any involvement in the murder by the police investigation, as no evidence linking them to the crime has been found. At one point during the course of investigation, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz noted that “DNA test results and polygraph test suggest that the murder and rape were committed by the servant.” However, he said the investigation was ongoing. On Oct 29, First Lady Aseefa Bhutto Zardari also met with Hina’s family at the Parliament and called for the family’s demand for a judicial commission to be “given due consideration”. Although Hina Javaid’s husband and her father-in-law were named in the initial FIR registered on murder charges, they were given a clean chit in the police investigation. However, Hina’s husband was arrested, while her father-in-law was only questioned by the police. It will be up to the court to decide whether Hina’s husband and father-in-law had any link to her murder. The police are required to submit a challan in a murder case within 15 days after a suspect is sent to judicial remand. Meanwhile, Hina’s family had expressed dissatisfaction over the police investigation and demanded a judicial inquiry. The family claimed to have proof of evidence tampering by the husband’s brother, who allegedly cleaned the accused’s room, tampered with evidence, and colluded with the police. The police have already added Section 376 of the Pakistan Penal Code (rape) to the case following the forensic DNA findings. CPO Sardar Ghias Gul told media persons that the challan had been submitted to the court for legal proceedings. He also acknowledged shortcomings in police prosecution, which result in the release of criminals, and said these would be addressed by appointing the right people to the right positions. The Punjab government had constituted a three-member high-powered committee to review the investigation into the murder case, in which her husband and a domestic servant had been placed on judicial remand at Adiala Jail. As part of the investigation, the committee also visited the crime scene, questioned the deceased woman’s husband and the domestic servant in jail, and met members of her family. The committee comprises Additional Inspector General of the Crime Control Department (CCD) Sohail Chattha, DIG Lahore Shoaib Khurram Janbaz and SSP Investigation Rawalpindi Saifullah. Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

items.title: COP 31: Africa expresses profound disappointment with outcomes, questions Presidency’s handling of negotiations
items.description: The African Group of Negotiators (AGN) has expressed profound disappointment with the outcomes of key negotiations at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, raising concerns over the substance of decisions and the process leading to their adoption. Speaking at the closing plenary, Chair of the African Group of Negotiators, Nana Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, said the outcomes on Action for Climate Empowerment (ACE) and long-term climate finance failed to adequately reflect Africa’s concerns and negotiating positions. COP31 closing plenary travelled to midnight on Saturday as negotiators remained deadlocked over whether the final agreement should explicitly address the phase-out of fossil fuels and provide support for vulnerable countries to adapt to climate change. In a statement on the outcome of negotiations on Action for Climate Empowerment, under agenda item 3(b) of COP31 and CMA 8, the African Group said it was disappointed with the proposed Action Plan for 2027–2031 under the Glasgow Work Programme. The Group said the proposed text failed to address its substantive concerns and clearly communicated red lines, despite its constructive engagement throughout the negotiations. It also questioned the role played by the COP31 Presidency, arguing that the process did not sufficiently reflect the responsibility of the Presidency to facilitate consensus among parties. “The Presidency’s responsibility is to facilitate consensus among Parties, in accordance with the rules of procedure, not to determine or impose an outcome on their behalf,” the Group stated. It insisted that the negotiations must remain party-driven, with the positions of all parties meaningfully considered in the development of final decisions. The African Group also raised concerns over the handling of negotiations on long-term climate finance, arguing that the process did not provide sufficient opportunity for parties to engage with the proposed decision. It said some paragraphs and provisions in the draft decision were not adequately negotiated, raising questions about the legitimacy and acceptability of the outcome. The Group further questioned the evidence base used in the assessment of the US$100 billion climate finance goal, noting that the information and key findings relied on only two sources. It said the consideration of Biennial Transparency Reports (BTRs) in the process was not given equal treatment by the Standing Committee on Finance (SCF). The African negotiators called for the SCF to develop a more robust methodological approach that would promote greater understanding and trust among parties in the assessment of climate finance provision and mobilisation. Despite its reservations, the Group indicated its willingness to adopt the decision on long-term finance if changes were made to paragraph three of the draft text to better reflect the realities of financial provision and mobilisation. It proposed that the paragraph be revised to avoid relying on references to key messages that, in its view, did not accurately capture the financial realities under consideration. The position reflects broader African concerns about the credibility of climate finance reporting, the fulfilment of commitments by developed countries and the need for decisions that translate into predictable support for developing countries. For Africa, the effectiveness of the climate negotiations depends not only on the adoption of decisions but also on whether the process is inclusive, transparent and responsive to the concerns of parties, particularly those most vulnerable to climate change. The African Group’s intervention at the closing plenary underscores its concern that consensus-building must not come at the expense of meaningful negotiations or the legitimate positions of developing countries. Africa’s position at COP31 had remained firm: “Implementation needs means of implementation” bearing in mind the realities of climate impacts on the continent’s peoples.

items.title: Kisseman–Christian Village bridge to close for six months for reconstruction
items.description: The bridge linking Kisseman and Christian Village in Accra will be closed to traffic for six months from the second week of December to allow for its reconstruction and elevation under the Greater Accra Resilient and Integrated Development (GARID) Project. The works are intended to improve the flow of rainwater through the area and reduce the risk of flooding during periods of heavy rainfall. GARID Project Communication Specialist, Philip Dunyo, said that alternative routes had been arranged to minimise the disruption to motorists who regularly use the busy road. He said drivers travelling from Achimota would be directed onto a route near a mosque before reaching the bridge, while those coming from Dome would use an alternative route at BJ Junction. “The road is a very busy road, and as a result, we have made alternative routes for motorists to use. As you can see the road is very busy. When you are coming from Achimota, there is a route leading to the mosque before you get here, so those coming from Achimota will use that side. Those coming from Dome, once they get to BJ junction, we have earmarked an alternative route there for them to use. We are blocking this road possibly by the second week of December,” he said. Residents of Kisseman and Christian Village have experienced recurring floods over the years, with incidents resulting in loss of lives, destruction of property and the displacement of some households. The existing bridge has been identified as one of the factors contributing to the flooding, as its narrow structure restricts the passage of water through the river during heavy downpours. He spoke to Channel one TV. The reconstruction and elevation are expected to address this bottleneck by improving water flow through the area. Motorists who use the bridge have been advised to take note of the planned closure and use the designated alternative routes during the construction period.

items.title: Prof Nunoo calls for automated fisheries management to curb political interference
items.description: Professor of Fisheries Science at the University of Ghana, Francis Kofi Ewusie Nunoo, has called for greater automation in Ghana’s fisheries sector, arguing that the use of modern technology could strengthen enforcement and reduce political interference in management decisions. He said the sector’s reliance on human decisions had weakened the enforcement of regulations and made it difficult for scientists and regulators to implement measures based on research evidence. Prof Nunoo believes technologies such as drones, satellites and artificial intelligence (AI) could improve monitoring, surveillance and enforcement, while reducing the scope for undue human influence. He made the remarks at the launch of his memoir, Tides and Waves of Grace: A Memoir , in Accra. He said fisheries management should be guided by scientific research, social considerations and economic data rather than political interests. “We scientists believe that we do management with science. So, whatever the science tells us, whatever the social and economic situation tells us, we have to use that data to do the management,” he said. Prof Nunoo noted that political interference had often undermined efforts by fisheries scientists to implement measures needed to protect fish stocks and ensure the long-term sustainability of the industry. He urged scientists and young professionals to uphold professional integrity and resist pressures that could compromise their work. He said researchers must have the courage to speak the truth and use evidence to influence national development, regardless of political or financial considerations. Prof Nunoo, who has spent nearly 30 years in academia and more than three decades in the fisheries sector, said his 204-page memoir documents the experiences, challenges and lessons that have shaped his personal and professional journey. Tides and Waves of Grace: A Memoir traces his childhood interest in fisheries, academic pursuits and professional experiences, including the difficulties he encountered on his path to becoming a professor. He said growing up along the coast influenced his decision to pursue fisheries, despite his parents’ initial preference for him to study medicine. The memoir, he explained, is intended to encourage younger people to remain determined in the face of challenges and to recognise the value of perseverance and faith. He also urged professionals and other individuals with meaningful experiences to document their stories to preserve knowledge and provide lessons for future generations. Prof Nunoo expressed concern about what he described as a declining reading culture, particularly among young people, and encouraged Ghanaians to develop greater interest in reading and writing books. He said the memoir was printed in Ghana as part of his commitment to supporting local industries and promoting locally produced goods and services. The book launch also featured discussions on climate change, its causes and possible interventions to address its environmental and economic consequences. Some senior lecturers and professors who participated in the discussions identified fossil fuel combustion, deforestation, industrial emissions, unsustainable agricultural practices and poor waste management as major contributors to climate change. They said the destruction of forest cover, the use of fossil fuels for energy and transportation, and emissions from industrial activities increase greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere, contributing to rising temperatures and changing weather patterns. The academics called for greater investment in renewable energy sources, including solar and wind power, as well as afforestation and reforestation programmes, sustainable agriculture and improved waste management. They also stressed the need for stronger environmental regulations, public education and climate-smart technologies to reduce emissions and improve communities’ resilience to climate-related disasters. The Head of the Department of Marine and Fisheries Sciences at the University of Ghana, Dr Benjamin Osei Botwe, described Prof Nunoo as an accomplished scholar, public servant, mentor and environmental advocate whose contributions extended beyond academia. He said Prof Nunoo had served in several leadership positions, including Head of Department, Chief Director at the Ministry of Fisheries and Aquaculture Development, Director of Tertiary Education at the Ministry of Education and Chairman of the Fisheries Commission. He had also served as Ghana’s Commissioner to the International Whaling Commission and Acting Deputy Director-General of the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission. Dr Botwe said Prof Nunoo’s work in research, marine conservation, public administration and the mentoring of younger academics had contributed to Ghana’s fisheries sector and higher education. He added that the memoir would preserve institutional knowledge while offering younger generations lessons in leadership, perseverance, public service and professional commitment.

items.title: 22-year-old Ghanaian man dies after apartment fire in New York
items.description: A 22-year-old Ghanaian man, identified as Zaidan Harun, has died after an apartment fire in the Soundview neighbourhood of the Bronx, New York. The fire broke out shortly after 12:20 p.m. on Thursday, November 19, 2026, at a residential building on Metcalf Avenue, according to reports by 12 Westchester. Fire officials said the blaze started on the second floor before spreading to the floor above. Harun, who lived in an apartment on the second floor, was rescued by firefighters and taken to Jacobi Medical Center, where he later died. Firefighters brought the blaze under control shortly after 1 p.m. Fire marshals have since begun investigations to establish what caused the fire. Harun was a former student of Al-Azhariya Islamic Senior High School in Kumasi. He reportedly moved to the United States in 2021 to further his education.

items.title: Summonses for India’s security czar, ex-spymaster sent to Delhi court
items.description: WASHINGTON: A US federal court has sent legal summonses for Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and former Research and Analysis Wing (R&AW) chief Samant Goel to three district courts in New Delhi, seeking assistance in serving them in a civil lawsuit alleging Indian government conspiracy to assassinate Sikh nationalist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun. US District Judge Katherine Polk Failla authorised the transmission of the legal documents through the Indian judicial system, after earlier attempts to serve them through India’s designated central authority and diplomatic channels failed. The summonses were sent by FedEx on Friday to Patiala House, Dwarka and Tis Hazari court complexes under provisions of the 1965 Hague Convention and India’s Code of Civil Procedure. The Patiala House district court was requested to facilitate service on Doval, while the Dwarka and Tis Hazari courts were approached in connection with Goel. US district judge allows alternative way after previous attempts failed in Pannun case The lawsuit, filed in September 2024, alleges that Indian officials conspired to arrange Pannun’s assassination in New York. It names the Indian government, Doval, Goel, former R&AW officer Vikram Yadav, Indian national Nikhil Gupta and 50 unidentified individuals as defendants. Pannun is seeking damages, alleging that the defendants conspired to arrange his assassination in retaliation for his advocacy of an independent Sikh state of Khalistan. The legal route was considered after the Indian Ministry of Law and Justice, the country’s designated central authority for processing foreign requests under the Hague Convention, returned the documents. The authority stated that the summonses did not fall within the specified categories. The US judge, however, held that the Indian authority’s brief response did not establish that the Hague Convention was inapplicable to the case. She concluded that Article 19 nevertheless permitted the use of India’s domestic judicial procedures. Previous attempts to serve Doval personally during his visits to the United States had also failed, according to court filings. Pannun’s lawyers told the court that security personnel had prevented them from delivering the documents on three occasions. While rejecting the lawsuit, India’s External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal reiterated New Delhi’s position, saying: “I have said earlier that we reject such baseless lawsuits.” Earlier on Nov 10, Jaiswal had described the allegations against senior Indian officials as fabricated and malicious and maintained that requests for serving judicial documents in India could only be routed through the Ministry of Law and Justice. The case has acquired renewed significance following the conviction and sentencing of Gupta in a separate US criminal proceeding on Friday. The federal court in New York sentenced Gupta to nearly 20 years in prison after he pleaded guilty in February 2026 to participating in a murder-for-hire conspiracy targeting Pannun. According to US prosecutors, Yadav, an Indian government employee associated with the Cabinet Secretariat that houses India’s intelligence service, had recruited Gupta in 2023 to arrange Pannun’s killing in New York. Prosecutors said Yadav agreed to pay $100,000 for the assassination, with $15,000 delivered as an advance payment. Gupta was arrested in the Czech Republic in June 2023 and extradited to the United States in 2024. Yadav has also been charged in the criminal case but remains outside US custody. Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

items.title: Punjab land reforms project reaches 90pc progress
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The World Bank-fin­a­n­ced Punjab Urban Land Systems Enhan­cement (Pulse) project has achieved 90 per cent physical progress, recording 69.9 million land rights in its information system against a target of 50.7 million, with 31pc registered in women’s names. According to the project’s progress report, all activities are expected to be completed by its closing date in June 2027. Updated digital cadastral maps now cover around 86pc of Punjab, while about 31 million person-based land records have been converted into parcel-based records. Of the province’s 6,014 revenue villages (mauzas), 5,805 have been digitised and notified, 27 have been submitted for notification and work remains in 182. World Bank-funded scheme digitises 5,805 revenue villages, with completion targeted for June 2027 The project covers more than 24.4m landowners. Under its mass partition initiative, 495,163 of the 1,747,071 eligible jointly owned land holdings have been divided, creating around 1.18m new parcels. Of these, 94,833 have been registered in women’s names. The Green Property Certificate survey has received 46,626 applications, completed 37,272 field assessments, approved 23,280 cases and issued 54,694 certificates. The project has also filled 346 positions across its management units. As of October, disbursements stood at around $91.84m, or 61.8pc of the total credit, the report said. Approved in 2022 with financing of $150m, the project aims to establish a unified land registry linked to digital cadastral maps, forming the basis of a comprehensive land administration system covering urban and rural areas of Punjab. Growing urban challenges The province has a population of around 110m, of which 36.7pc lives in urban areas. Urban growth is largely driven by migration from rural areas, with 60pc of recent migrants to Punjab’s urban centres coming from rural areas. The report identifies several environmental and social challenges in urban and peri-urban areas, including air pollution, contaminated drinking water, untreated wastewater, inadequate solid waste collection and disposal, and the expansion of cities over prime agricultural land. It also highlights public health probl­e­ms, particularly water-borne diseases, unequal access to basic services, weak tra­nsparency and accountability, and low public satisfaction with service delivery. Government agencies lack up-to-date information about public land that could be used for housing and other developm­ent projects. Land acquisition can take up to five years on average, it says. Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

items.title: Referendum is no substitute for legislation: PTI
items.description: • Challenges Bilawal to return reserved seats, remove Kundi • Accuses PPP leadership of playing ‘good cop, bad cop’ ISLAMABAD: The PTI on Saturday dismissed proposals for a referendum on new provinces as an absurd and futile exercise that could not replace a majority vote or a constitutional bill in the national or provincial assemblies, while urging PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari to return reserved seats to the party and remove Faisal Karim Kundi as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa governor. In a statement, PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram said floating the idea of a referendum instead of introducing legislation in parliament validated the party’s long-standing position that the sitting assemblies lacked legitimacy and had been formed on a “stolen mandate and usurped seats” through Form-47 results. “Because the current lawmakers are not true public representatives, any referendum held under the present setup would be as fraudulent as the assembly itself,” he claimed. Outlining the PTI’s internal consultation process, Mr Akram said the issue of a referendum would be deliberated upon by the parliamentary party, political committee and core committee, though the final authority rested solely with incarcerated PTI founder Imran Khan. He made it clear that the PTI would formulate its policy on the creation of new provinces only after party leaders were granted direct access to Imran Khan, whose approval would be final. He noted that while Imran Khan and the PTI had consistently advocated smaller administrative units, the party would never endorse decisions imposed without constitutional legitimacy, democratic consensus and public consent. He warned that imposing governments on people who had rejected them would defeat the purpose of administrative reform. The PTI information secretary expressed gratitude to Mr Bhutto-Zardari for expressing concern over the health of Imran Khan, demanding his release and calling him a political prisoner. He said the PTI thanked all those who had spoken out against the “unjust” treatment meted out to the party founder. Turning his attention to the PPP leadership, Mr Akram said President Asif Ali Zardari had always engaged in the politics of expediency and claimed that the father-son duo was currently playing a good cop, bad cop routine that the public recognised well. While acknowledging the PPP chairman’s recent, belated admission of harsh political realities, he stressed that words alone could not establish credibility without a clear break from the government’s “unconstitutional” measures. Challenge to Bilawal To prove his sincerity and show that his remarks were not merely an attempt to extract political concessions or a greater share in government, Mr Akram challenged Mr Bhutto-Zardari to take two immediate confidence-building measures: ensure the return of all usurped reserved seats to the PTI and remove Faisal Karim Kundi as KP governor or expel him from the PPP to prove that the party no longer supported measures against the province’s elected government. He argued that the PPP could not absolve itself of responsibility for the coercion and mistreatment faced by the PTI while remaining part of the ruling arrangement. Reflecting on the past three years, Mr Akram said systematic electoral manipulation, undue interference and controversial constitutional amendments had virtually paralysed parliament and the judiciary. He noted that even a major government ally had refused to openly endorse the amendments. Genuine democratic change, he emphasised, required respect for the people’s electoral mandate, ensuring that parliament served the public and allowing the judiciary to rule on merit. He condemned the disappearance of former KP finance minister Taimur Saleem Jhagra from a police station following his arrest, alongside the arrests of Irfan Saleem and Kamran Bangash, calling these incidents an extreme manifestation of lawlessness. He reiterated the PTI’s demand that Imran Khan, his wife Bushra Bibi, non-functional KP chief minister Sohail Afridi, provincial assembly speaker Babar Saleem Swati, former Gilgit-Baltistan chief minister Khalid Khurshid Khan, Taimur Saleem Jhagra and all other detained leaders and workers be immediately presented before the courts and released without delay. He asserted that they were being targeted solely for upholding constitutional supremacy and the rule of law. Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

items.title: Focus on public issues, avoid new fault lines: PPP
items.description: President Asif Ali Zardari meets with Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar and National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq at the Presidency.—X/PresOfPakistan ISLAMABAD: Seeking to ease tensions between her party and PML-N amid the ongoing debate on need for new provinces, PPP Vice President Senator Sherry Rehman on Saturday urged the government to focus on people’s problems rather than create new political fault lines. Provocative statements by ministers should be avoided, she said, adding that PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari wanted politics to address people’s problems rather than create new divisions. “Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari is looking to prevent bloodshed, not shed it,” she said. Her statement came before Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar and National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq met President Asif Ali Zardari at President House to discuss the overall political situation. Besides Senator Rehman, PPP leader Raja Pervez Ashraf was also present. The meeting followed an apparent easing of tensions between President Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif who also discussed the matter with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi after the PPP chairman’s remarks at a ‘Meet the Press’ event at the Karachi Press Club. He had opposed the creation of new provinces, warning that dividing Sindh would lead to bloodshed. He also criticised the coalition over several issues, including the treatment of JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, PTI founder Imran Khan’s incarceration and the 27th Amendment. He later clarified that he was raising an alarm, not issuing a threat, and complained that the PPP was not being consulted. The remarks drew sharp reactions from PML-N ministers Khawaja Asif and Tallal Chaudhry, while MQM-P chief Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui urged the courts to take notice. Mustafa Kamal also criticised Mr Bhutto-Zardari. President Zardari subsequently met Prime Minister Shehbaz and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, with the meeting calling for dialogue and restraint in public statements. A separate PPP meeting reaffirmed the party’s opposition to Sindh’s division. A meeting between Mr Bhutto-Zardari and the prime minister is also expected in the coming days. Senator Rehman also warned of a difficult winter, with gas and resource shortages and extreme weather in many areas, urging politicians not to add to people’s troubles by creating new fault lines. Constitutional process She also drew a constitutional line on demands by some ministers for a referendum on new provinces. “They [the ministers] should know that the Constitution will still refer the matter to parliament. There is no walking away from the votes of the assemblies. A referendum does not override the Constitution, nor does it change any ground reality where any given province has spoken with its majority,” she said. The PPP’s message was that it wanted the truce to hold but would oppose the creation of new provinces outside the constitutional parliamentary process. Whether the easing of tensions lasts will depend on whether the parties pursue consultation and consensus through parliament or revive the referendum debate. Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

items.title: Chinese airport volunteer bridges cultures one hello at a time
items.description: The age-old saying that when one door closes, another opens rings true for 33-year-old Song Xiangcai, originally from Jinan in east China's Shandong Province. After moving to Shanghai in 2017, he started working in the internet industry as a product manager and later advanced to senior product manager. A few years later, however, he was laid off during a company-wide restructuring. He didn't know it at the time, but that closed door would open up opportunities to learn new languages, meet people from across the world and gain online popularity. After seeing videos online of others doing volunteer work at airports, he thought it would be a great opportunity to meet new people and improve his English-speaking skills. But the move from the corporate world to volunteer work came with sacrifices, especially financially. "I don't get paid as a volunteer. From the very beginning, and even now, I have to cover the costly round-trip fares to the airport myself, and food there is also expensive," he told CGTN during an interview. "At first, I relied on my savings from my previous job. Later, I gained some traffic and started earning revenue from it. I also got a few small commercial sponsorships, which brought in advertising income. Right now, this income covers my living expenses, though I still make considerably less than I did when I worked as a product manager." A turning point came in November last year, when Song decided to document his volunteer journey online. Now, scrolling through his videos, posted across Chinese social media apps, it's like Song doesn't belong anywhere else. His friendly encounters with strangers are endearing and make for an easy watch. He offers help to visitors in a foreign country where language is often a barrier, giving directions, helping panicked travelers find their lost phones or simply saying a kind hello. Along the way, he's also picked up different languages through these interactions. "I started learning English when I began volunteering last year. Later, I picked up Russian, Japanese, Korean and Spanish. I only master practical phrases for volunteer work in these languages, enough to help people with basic issues like directions. My English is far more advanced," he said. Knowing even a few phrases in another language has proved useful. "Not every foreign visitor to China speaks English. I've found many only know their native language. Knowing a few extra languages makes communication much easier," Song said. He hopes to add German, French, Portuguese, Thai and Arabic to his repertoire, along with various Chinese dialects and sign language. The exchanges also go both ways. He has taught visitors simple Chinese and shared videos of them using what they have learned to help Chinese people. Despite these rewarding exchanges, his move into volunteering wasn't initially well received by everyone. His family weren't supportive at first, concerned about his financial well-being. "I just got married last year and need to take responsibility for our family. But as my content grew popular and gradually started covering part of our living costs, my family came to understand and support what I do." The online attention has come as a surprise to Song. Although his videos draw both positive and negative comments, he says the overall response has been uplifting. But what keeps him returning to the airport is the joy he finds in helping others. Not every encounter is pleasant, but he says the happy moments far outweigh the difficult ones. "I feel that when I help others, my body releases dopamine and endorphins. These chemicals lift my mood, and it's almost addictive. That's why I look forward to every trip. The sincere responses from those I assist can keep me happy for a long time," he said. Beyond helping cover his living expenses, Song wants his videos to offer a window into everyday life in China. Through ordinary encounters with visitors, he hopes international viewers will see the warmth and kindness of Chinese people, as well as the country's diversity. "I want to show how ordinary Chinese interact naturally with international visitors in English. I hope to counter biased videos that smear China, so the world can see the real China," he said. For him, that means keeping the encounters authentic. "I showcase the real China through genuine interactions, instead of staged and rehearsed videos," he said. He also hopes Chinese viewers will learn about other cultures and pick up English and other languages along the way. Looking ahead, Song plans to keep learning languages and improving his English, while finding more opportunities to connect people across cultures. "I hope to promote Chinese globally and get chances to do meaningful work that contributes to cross-cultural communication," he said.

items.title: IRGC targets US radars in Bahrain as Trump seeks 'permanent deal'
items.description: US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Saturday that he wants a "permanent" deal that stops Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. He said Iranian officials are "very, very difficult." The Iranian side has not yet responded to Trump's statement but has expressed willingness to keep dialogue open. Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday that the current diplomatic efforts "must be given a chance, and the blockade must be lifted rationally." "Our position is clear: as long as Iran's demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless," he said. "At the same time, we have always affirmed our readiness for dialogue, just as we are ready to defend ourselves," he added. Iran fights an economic war While media coverage of the US-Iran conflict has focused on the security risks in the Strait of Hormuz and military exchanges between the two sides, Iran has recently said it is also fighting on a less visible front. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Saturday that the country is engaged in a "silent" economic war, "which is far more difficult than a conflict involving the launching of missiles and destruction," according to the official news agency IRNA. He said at a conference in Tehran that the "enemy" had expected to cause a famine in the country and a shortage of goods in the domestic market but had failed to achieve its objectives. He added that Iran's "wheels of production continue to turn," while stressing that the economic war waged by the United States was certainly not simple. He added that Iran's security and military forces had responded with strength, while calling for greater national unity and solidarity in the face of the "enemy's invasions and unequal war." Ongoing military conflict Iran's Army also claimed that its homegrown air defense systems based in the country's southern regions fired missiles at a US F-16 fighter jet on Friday night over the Gulf, forcing it to make an emergency landing at an airport in a regional state. US Central Command later rejected this account, stating that "Iran did not attack a US F-16 fighter aircraft yesterday - at all." Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) also said Saturday night that its aerospace force had targeted US radar systems at two air bases in Bahrain in retaliatory missile and drone strikes. The "hybrid offensive" operation was in response to the continuation of the "aggression against and violation" of Iran's airspace and targeted the Al-Riffa and Awali Sakhir air bases in Bahrain, the IRGC said in a statement on its official news outlet Sepah News. The IRGC warned that Iran's airspace is a red line for the country's armed forces and that any violation by a state or aggressive force would receive a "harsh and decisive" response. (With input from Xinhua)

items.title: Trump intends to secure ‘permanent deal’ with Iran
items.description: • Araghchi says Tehran seeks ‘honourable, dignified’ agreement; says China, Russia oppose change in nuclear doctrine • Trump envoys discuss mediation with Qatari officials • Two tankers catch fire in Strait of Hormuz WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump has said he intends to secure a “permanent” deal with Iran, insisting that no future American president should be able to allow Tehran to obtain a nuclear weapon, according to an Anadolu Agency report. Speaking in a phone interview with Fox News on Saturday, Trump said his approach was shaped by what he described as “Iran’s repeated failure” to honour agreements. “We make a deal, and then they break the deal the next day,” he said, arguing that any new agreement must prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons regardless of who occupies the White House in the coming years. Reuters quoted the US president as telling Fox News that he’s “going to make a deal that is permanent”. He added that he would not allow a fut­ure administration to reverse course and permit Iran to acquire a nuclear weapon. Trump also addressed suggestions that Washington was pursuing regime change in Tehran, saying his administration had already dealt with successive groups of Iranian leadership. “We’re dealing with the third group, so you could call that the ultimate regime change,” he said, adding that the current figures were “probably … more reasonable” but remained difficult to negotiate with. Guarantees sought On the other hand, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told the state-owned Iran newspaper that messages continued to be exchanged between Tehran and Washington through mediators, and that Tehran was seeking “an agreement that would ensure there was no further war”. He also said Iran wanted guarantees that Washington was serious about negotiations before proceeding further, adding that Iran had discussed with mediators the form and nature of confidence-building measures. He also said China and Russia oppose a change in Tehran’s nuclear doctrine, amid domestic calls for a shift. He told the state-run Iran Daily that the issue was “broad, serious” and had its own “supporters and opponents”. “Russia and China are also opposed” to a change in Iran’s doctrine, he added. The remarks came as diplomatic efforts by Qatar continued to try to end a conflict that has destabilised the Middle East, disrupted shipping, driven up global energy prices and drawn in countries across the region. The foreign minister said Iran’s red lines included keeping its highly enriched uranium in the country, though he said a “fair solution” was still possible. He said Iran remains open to diplomacy with the United States but would not accept an agreement that compromises its dignity or undermines the victory it has achieved on the battlefield, IRNA reports. Araghchi said Tehran was seeking a “good, honourable and dignified agreement,” stressing that any deal must safeguard Iran’s national interests and prevent a renewed conflict. “We are seeking an agreement that would ensure there is no more war afterwards.” US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner earlier met senior Qatari officials in Berlin on Thursday to discuss mediation efforts between the US and Iran, Axios reports according to Reuters, citing two sources with knowledge of the meeting. Two tankers caught fire Meanwhile, two tankers caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, at the heart of the conflict between Iran and the US. “A tanker transiting outbound in the Strait of Hormuz has been hit on the stern by an unknown projectile. There are no reported casualties at this time,” the British maritime agency UKMTO stated. Also, Iran said it shot down a US drone over Qeshm Island in the strait, according to Iranian state TV. Araghchi has said reopening the Strait of Hormuz is “not difficult”, but requires the US to accept “reasonable conditions” under international law and acknowledge its “mistakes” and previous commitments, Al Jazeera reports. Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

items.title: Textile exports rise 6.35pc in July-October
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Pakistan’s textile and clothing exports grew by 6.35 per cent to $6.797 billion in July-October 2026–27, from $6.391bn in the corresponding period last year. The modest rise in export proceeds was attributed to elevated input costs, which eroded exporters’ competitiveness, and external shocks that disrupted shipments, according to data from the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics. The suspension of trade with Afghanistan since October 2025 and falling exports to the Middle East, especially the United Arab Emirates, due to the ongoing war in the region, were the key reasons for slow export growth. High cost, war shocks and Afghan trade halt slow growth; oil import bill jumps on higher crude prices The PBS data showed exports of readymade garments rose 13.91pc in value and 17.62pc in quantity during July-October FY27, while knitwear increased 3.97pc in value and 5.63pc in quantity. By contrast, bedwear dipped 0.70pc in value and 1.98pc in quantity. Towel exports rose 10.06pc in value and 9.74pc in quantity in 4MFY27, whereas cotton cloth dipped 4.44pc in value and 6.06pc in quantity, respectively. Yarn exports surged 30.17pc in 4MFY27. Exports of made-up articles, excluding towels, increased by 10.76pc, while tents, canvas, and tarpaulin fell by 34.07pc in 4MFY27. Imports of synthetic fibre decreased by 14.40pc in 4MFY27, while the arrival of synthetic and artificial silk yarn rose by 9.06pc in 4MFY27. Imports of raw cotton increased 21.55pc in 4MFY27. However, arrival of second-hand clothes surged 22.52pc during the period year on year. Rice exports Negative growth was recorded in non-basmati rice exports in October in both quantity and value over the last year. Non-basmati exports dipped 3.27pc in value and 7.68pc in quantity in October on a year-on-year basis. However, basmati exports grew 21.85pc in value and 18.39pc in quantity in October. During the July-October period, exports of basmati rice surged 69.07pc and non-basmati by 27.03pc in value year on year. The increase was also noted in quantity for both basmati (64.79pc) and non-basmati (28.53pc), respectively. The Ministry of Commerce has extended the subsidy scheme for rice exports by another three months until Sept 30 and raised the Duty Drawback of Local Taxes and Levies (DLTL) rate for non-basmati rice to support exporters facing weaker international demand. Analysts linked the decline in non-basmati rice exports to the discontinuation of DLTL, as Pakistani rice is uncompetitive compared to Indian rice in the international market. Oil imports Pakistan’s oil import bill rose 9.34pc in 4MFY27 to $5.630bn from $5.149bn a year ago. Data showed that crude oil imports increased by 33.07pc in value, with a decline of 8.37pc in quantity, indicating that the higher value is due to rising international oil prices. The value of petroleum products increased by 10.62pc, while quantity declined by 24.02pc in 4MFY27 year on year. On the other hand, imports of liq­uefied natural gas declined by 47.19pc, while imports of liquefied petroleum gas grew by 18.88pc, ref­lecting demand for energy products. Imports under the telecommunication group decreased by 7.30pc year on year, mainly due to a decline in other mobile phone imports in 4MFY27. Mobile handset imports declined by 7.20pc in the first four months of the current fiscal year compared with the same period last year. Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

items.title: In an Egypt village, generations of Palestinians denied a normal life
items.description: Shamma Abu Hussein is possibly the last person in her village of refugees to have lived in historic Palestine. Living in Egypt, she has watched three generations of her family grow up in legal limbo. She was among the hundreds of thousands who fled or were expelled during the creation of the State of Israel in 1948, whose descendants number in the millions. Now she fears that the effects of the Gaza war and rhetoric from Israeli ministers calling for Gazans to be expelled means history is repeating itself.

items.title: COP31 closing session ends, outcome document expected over weekend
items.description: Negotiators at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) wrapped up a late-night closing plenary around midnight on Friday, with the final outcome document expected to be released over the weekend. "Our responsibility now is to deliver results, and I believe we will achieve that result in this hall. Very little distance remains," COP31 President Murat Kurum said at the closing session in Antalya. Kurum urged delegations to focus on consensus rather than individual priorities after days of intensive consultations, expressing hope that parties would leave with an "Antalya Consensus." On Friday, COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen said negotiators would continue working "for as long as it takes to get the job done," and that there was "a spirit of goodwill" among delegations. Discussions on the latest draft texts have focused on climate finance, adaptation support, clean energy, electrification and carbon capture. Opening on November 9, COP31 brought together representatives from nearly 200 parties to focus on delivering on climate pledges.

items.title: SMOKERS’ CORNER: The Migration Paradox
items.description: Till the early 1970s, it was often believed that South Asians who travelled to Western countries for studies or migrated there, often adopted ‘Western values.’ In early Indian and Pakistani movies, Pakistanis and Indians returning from the West were often portrayed as enlightened, rational people who scoffed at the superstitious beliefs of their countrymen and women. By the mid-1970s, though, the portrayal of West-returned Pakistanis and Indians changed. They began being portrayed as stupid, dope-smoking, guitar-slinging hippies. But in the decades that followed, reality turned out very differently. Instead of becoming less religious or adopting ‘immoral’ lifestyles, many South Asians living abroad actually became much more religious than their relatives back home. Anyone travelling between major South Asian cities and the suburbs of Western cities can see this contrast. In South Asia, religion is a natural part of everyday life, heard in the call to prayer or seen at local temples. People do not have to work hard to keep it alive. Abroad, however, mosque and temple attendance becomes stricter, food rules become more rigid, and dogmatic religious rules often replace the relaxed, mixed traditions practised back home. According to the American anthropologist Steven Vertovec, moving to a new country rarely weakens religious belief. Instead, it often makes people more conscious of their faith. This change happens because of a deep desire to protect one’s culture, and the political reality of living as a minority in a foreign land. Leaving South Asia means leaving behind extended families, friends, familiar streets and unspoken social rules. In Western countries, society focuses heavily on individual independence and small nuclear families, which can make newcomers feel lonely. Religion fills this void. South Asian immigrant communities in the secular West have often developed stricter religious identities than their counterparts back home. What explains this paradox? According to the Terror Management Theory developed by psychologists Jeff Greenberg, Sheldon Solomon and Tom Pyszczynski, when people feel anxious because their familiar world has disappeared, they hold on tighter to their core beliefs to feel secure. The mosque, temple or the gurdwara in a Western country offers this, more than they do in the homeland of the immigrants. In his book Religions of Immigrants from India and Pakistan, the American sociologist Raymond B. Williams posits that religious outlets abroad become the main places where immigrants reinstate their otherwise unsure presence. Inside these spaces, they are no longer treated as outsiders. According to multiple surveys by the Pew Research Centre, daily prayers and rituals act as emotional anchors that connect immigrants to their ‘heritage.’ Illustration by Abro Back in South Asia, a person’s identity is naturally supported by local languages, movies, food and festivals. One does not need to visit a temple to feel Indian, or a mosque to feel Pakistani as such, because the whole society reinforces that identity. Abroad, however, the pressure to blend in is strong, indicated by the fear shown in 1970s Urdu and Hindi movies about ‘Westernised’ youth. Worried that their children will forget their roots, immigrant parents use special religious classes outside the curriculum in secular Western countries. The British scholar Pnina Werbner, in her studies of British Pakistanis, talks about a “cultural freeze.” While people in South Asia continue to debate, modernise and change their views over time, immigrant communities often freeze the religious and social rules of the exact decade they left. A family that left Lahore or Ahmedabad in the 1980s might strictly follow conservative rules that their own cousins back home are likely to have moved away from. The Pakistani-American historian Ayesha Jalal and the French scholar Olivier Roy point out that the blended traditions of South Asia do not travel well. According to Roy’s idea of “deculturation”, when religion is separated from its home soil, what survives is a simpler, literalist and stricter version of it. Becoming more religious abroad is also driven by politics, shaped by political tensions brought over from South Asia. In many Western countries, especially under multicultural policies, governments organise immigrant groups by their religion rather than their language or region. As the British-Pakistani political sociologist Tariq Modood has demonstrated, British citizens from South Asia quickly realised that local councils, politicians and the media in the West do not deal with them as members of an ethnic group, but as ‘British Muslims’, ‘American Hindus’ or ‘Canadian Sikhs.’ Due to the fact that the government recognises general religious labels, people have a strong reason to organise around their faith if they want a political voice. At the same time, rising prejudice, Islamophobia and anti-immigrant attitudes trigger what American sociologists Alejandro Portes and Rubén Rumbaut call “reactive religion.” According to their research, when a minority group feels judged, turning toward religion becomes a way to defend themselves. Wearing visible religious symbols such as a hijab, a turban or a tilak becomes a public statement of strength — at least to the wearers. This is made even stronger by what the Irish political scientist Benedict Anderson terms as “long-distance nationalism.” Free from the daily struggles of living in South Asia, many immigrants develop an idealised version of their homeland, or what it ought to be like. The American anthropologist Arjun Appadurai explains in his book Modernity at Large that television and social media bring the bitter religious/sectarian/communal conflicts of South Asia straight into immigrant living rooms. With more money to spare and a desire to prove their loyalty to their home country, some people abroad eagerly fund religious groups and political parties back home, taking part in homeland politics from a safe distance. The old movie image of the modern, non-religious ‘West-returned’ traveller gave way to fears of ‘Western immorality’ and finally to a reality where immigrants became more conservative and orthodox. But here’s the irony: many South Asians leave their countries looking for better jobs, fair laws and personal freedom. Yet, once they arrive in secular countries, they often rebuild the exact religious walls they left behind. According to Vertovec, migration to secular Western democracies does not secularise South Asians. Instead, it prompts them to self-consciously institutionalise and reconstruct sharper religious boundaries than those they navigated back home. Interestingly, as South Asian cities expand, their growing middle classes face the same pressures that shaped immigrants in London or Houston. Moving away from joint families into small nuclear arrangements, many among the middle classes have increasingly begun to rely on structured programmes, such as Quran academies and Sunday Bal Vihar classes. This shift is accelerated by digital media and what anthropologist Peggy Levitt terms “social remittances” or the flow of ideas and behaviours from migrants back to their homelands. Post-1980s Bollywood costume dramas set inside joint families and recent Pakistani ‘morality serials’ are examples of this shift. In these, lifestyle modernity is woven into an idealised portrayal of faith. The rational West-returned man or the silly hippie is long gone, systematically replaced by good looking middle class believers who have ‘rediscovered’ their faith. Even though faith in India or Pakistan was never in any danger of getting lost. Published in Dawn, EOS, November 22nd, 2026

items.title: Journalist’s bail plea rejected
items.description: QUETTA: A local court in Quetta on Saturday rejected the bail application of Islamabad-based journalist Shahid Maitla. The bail application was filed by Rahib Buledi Advocate and other lawyers in the court of Judicial Magistrate-VII. Judicial Magistrate Akhtar Shah, who had reserved the verdict on the application, announced the decision. Shahid Maitla was arrested under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca) on a complaint lodged by former caretaker prime minister Anwarul Haq Kakar. After his arrest, Shahid Maitla was shifted from Islamabad to Quetta.He is currently on judicial remand in District Jail, Quetta. Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

items.title: Eleven books handed over to Adiala jail authorities for Imran
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Eleven books covering a diverse range of subjects have been handed over to Adiala jail authorities for PTI founder and former prime minister Imran Khan to read. Khalid Yousaf Chaudhry, who regularly visits jails and courts in connection with Mr Khan’s legal and prison-related matters, confirmed that the books had been handed over to the authorities. “The books cover a variety of subjects, including world and ancient history, Islamic history, Islamic law and jurisprudence, religion, philosophy, Sufism, political thought, international relations, diplomacy and global affairs,” he said. The collection also includes works on the rise and fall of civilisations, the evolution of Islamic thought, Muslim history, colonial-era legal de­­velopments, international power politics, wars and global political developments, he added. “The selection offers a broad range of historical, religious, intellectual and political perspectives, reflecting diverse areas of academic and literary interest.” Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

items.title: Jospong subsidiary partners Turkish firm to test shrimp-shell-based farm products in Ghana
items.description: The African Agribusiness Consortium Limited (AAC), a subsidiary of the Jospong Group of Companies, has signed a memorandum of understanding with Türkiye-based ChitoGlobal Biotechnology to test agricultural products derived from discarded shrimp and crab shells on farms in Ghana. Signed on the sidelines of COP31 in Antalya, the agreement will begin with joint research and field trials to assess the products’ suitability for Ghanaian farming conditions. The products are based on chitosan, a substance derived from chitin, which is naturally found in the shells of crustaceans. The trials will examine whether the products can protect seeds and plants, improve crop resilience during dry spells and strengthen plants’ natural defences against fungal diseases. They will also assess the products’ effects on soil quality and crop yields, as well as their potential to provide farmers with a more affordable alternative to some conventional agricultural inputs. After the signing, Jospong Group Chief Investment and Innovation Officer Noah Gyimah said the company would work with Ghana’s environmental and standards authorities to ensure the products meet local regulatory requirements before introducing them for use on its farms. “Our joint efforts will transition this technology from research and development to practical application. We will commence with collaborative research and field trials in Ghana, followed by technology transfer and full-scale commercial production,” he said. Mr Gyimah said the pilot would also help AAC assess the commercial viability of the products, identify potential buyers and determine whether Ghana has sufficient raw materials to support local production. He said the consortium intends to make the products available to smallholder farmers if the trials establish their suitability. AAC also plans to assess their potential use in growing its own crops and vegetables on a commercial scale for the Ghanaian market. The agreement followed a visit by a four-member AAC delegation, led by the consortium’s Coordinator, Dr Emmanuel Volsuuri, to ChitoGlobal’s facility in Antalya. Dr Volsuuri said he arranged the visit after meeting the company at its COP31 pavilion, where further discussions led to the opportunity to examine its operations and technology first-hand. The delegation toured the facility to learn about the composition of the products and the operations of the company’s laboratories. Dr Volsuuri said the visit helped AAC assess the products’ potential to support crop disease management and improve soil health in Ghana. He also cited concerns about the widespread use of conventional chemical treatments in agriculture and the need to explore alternatives that could reduce farmers’ reliance on them. AAC Chief Executive, Dr Adelaide Araba Siaw Agyepong, leads the consortium, which grows rice, maize, vegetables and soybeans commercially in Ghana. The company also supports farmers with access to mechanisation services, financing and markets. ChitoGlobal Biotechnology develops biopolymer products for agricultural and medical applications. ChitoGlobal Sales and Technical Support Manager, Dana Abourahma, said the partnership would combine the expertise of both organisations. “This collaboration brings together extensive local knowledge with cutting-edge scientific capabilities,” she said. The proposed research and field trials will determine whether the chitosan-based products can be adapted for Ghanaian farms and whether local production could be commercially viable.

items.title: Haruna Iddrisu announces €325m loan plan to address water shortages in three Northern cities
items.description: Education Minister and Tamale South MP, Haruna Iddrisu, says a €325 million loan agreement to support water infrastructure projects in Tamale, Damongo and Yendi will be laid before Parliament next week. He made the announcement at a ceremony in Tamale organised by members of Ahlussunna wal Jama’a (ASWAJ) to celebrate the selection of Sheikh Ibrahim Basha Iddris, popularly known as Sheikh Bayaan, as the group’s interim National Imam. Addressing the gathering, Mr Iddrisu said Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson would present the agreement to Parliament. “Next week, the Finance Minister, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, will lay before Parliament a loan agreement of 325 million euros to end the water crisis in Tamale, Damongo, and Yendi,” he said. The proposed financing is expected to support major water infrastructure development in the three municipalities, where residents have experienced persistent challenges with reliable water supply. If approved by Parliament, the loan would provide funding for the planned interventions, although details of the project components, implementation timeline and expected completion dates were not provided in the announcement. The proposed investment is intended to improve access to potable water for households, businesses and public institutions in the beneficiary communities. Iddrisu welcomes Sheikh Bayaan’s selection The Education Minister also described Sheikh Bayaan’s selection as interim National Imam of ASWAJ as a significant moment for the organisation and the wider Muslim community. He expressed hope that the new leader’s tenure would contribute to the advancement of Islamic education in Ghana. “The choice of Sheikh Bayaan to lead ASWAJ as National Imam is a proud moment, and I am hopeful that his reign will be remembered for his enormous contribution to Islamic education in the country,” he said. The ceremony brought together members of ASWAJ in Tamale, who gathered to celebrate Sheikh Bayaan and pledge their allegiance to his leadership.

items.description: By Sarah McFarlane and Peter Hobson ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 22 (Reuters) - UN climate talks collapsed on Sunday as the European Union and others rejected a final draft deal put forward by COP31 presidents Turkey and Australia, saying it was too weak to advance the fight against global warming. The failed talks reflect world governments' struggle this year to muster ambitious action to address the worsening consequences of climate change, as wars, economic pressures and other crises compete for their attention.

items.title: All 16 regional best farmers to receive pick-up vehicles at 2026 Farmers’ Day
items.description: All 16 regional best farmers will receive brand-new pick-up vehicles at this year’s National Farmers’ Day celebration, the Minister of Food and Agriculture, Eric Opoku, has announced. The national best farmer with a disability will also receive a pick-up vehicle and GH¢200,000 at the 42nd edition of the celebration, scheduled for Friday, December 4, 2026, at the University of Energy and Natural Resources (UENR) in Sunyani. Mr Opoku announced the awards during a courtesy call on the Paramount Chief of the Sunyani Traditional Area, Odeefour Ogyeamansan Boahen Korkor II, at the Nana Bosoma Royal Palace in Asufufu, a suburb of Sunyani. The visit was to formally invite the traditional ruler to chair the opening session of the national celebration. The minister described this year’s event as exceptional, noting that it would mark the 42nd anniversary of National Farmers’ Day, which was instituted in 1984. He also disclosed that all former national best farmers since the inception of the awards had been invited to attend the celebration, although four of them had passed away. Odeefour Ogyeamansan Boahen Korkor II welcomed the minister’s visit and pledged the support of the chiefs and people of Sunyani towards the successful organisation of the event.
